Food Allergies (Psychosomatik-Register · Immune System & Autoimmune)
An immune system that senses a threat in the very thing meant to nourish.
Definition: In a food allergy, the immune system reacts to otherwise harmless protein components of certain foods with an excessive defense response, usually mediated by specific IgE antibodies. On renewed contact with the allergen, histamine and other messenger substances are released within minutes to hours, which can trigger symptoms in the skin, mucous membranes, gastrointestinal tract, or airways. Common triggers are nuts, milk, egg, fish, soy, wheat, and certain fruits, with sensitivity varying widely between individuals. A true allergy must be distinguished from a food intolerance, which does not involve an immune mechanism but rather, for example, an enzyme deficiency. The reasons for the markedly rising frequency in recent decades are suspected to include, among other things, changed eating habits, excessive hygiene, and correspondingly less-trained gut flora.
Typische Symptome: Itching and tingling in the mouth and throat; Hives (wheals) and skin redness; Nausea, abdominal cramps, diarrhea; Swelling of lips, tongue, or throat; Sneezing and runny nose; Breathing difficulties up to a feeling of chest tightness; In severe cases, anaphylactic shock
Notfall-Hinweis: For shortness of breath, swelling of the tongue or throat, circulatory collapse, or loss of consciousness, call emergency services immediately – this can be a life-threatening anaphylactic shock requiring emergency medication (adrenaline).
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.

Sarcoidosis (Psychosomatik-Register · Immune System & Autoimmune)
A silent inflammation that settles into small nodules in tissue – often unnoticed for years.
Definition: Sarcoidosis is an inflammatory systemic disease in which small clusters of immune cells, called granulomas, form in various organs. Most often affected are the lungs and lymph nodes in the chest, but skin, eyes, liver, heart, or the nervous system can also be involved. The disease is thought to arise from an excessive immune response to a trigger not yet reliably identified, in people with a corresponding genetic predisposition. Many courses are mild and heal on their own within a few years, while others become chronic and can lead to lasting scarring in the tissue. Characteristic is that the disease often initially causes barely noticeable, nonspecific complaints and is frequently discovered only by chance, for instance during an X-ray.
Typische Symptome: Dry cough and breathing difficulties; Persistent tiredness and fatigue; Swollen lymph nodes; Mild fever and night sweats; Skin changes, such as painful reddish nodules on the shins; Joint pain; Visual disturbances with eye involvement

Breast Cancer (Psychosomatik-Register · Oncology)
The most common cancer in women – its origin is not directly connected to personality, but the way diagnosis, body image, and treatment are handled does vary.
Definition: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women, though in rare cases it can also affect men. It arises from the uncontrolled proliferation of malignant cells in breast tissue, usually starting in the milk ducts (ductal) or the glandular lobules (lobular). The disease is biologically very heterogeneous: there are hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-positive, and triple-negative subtypes that differ greatly in aggressiveness and treatment response. Known risk factors include age, genetic predisposition (including BRCA1/2 mutations), hormonal influences, family history, and lifestyle factors – but the exact cause is multifactorial and, for most people affected, cannot be traced to a single origin. Thanks to early detection (mammography, self-examination) and improved therapies, the prognosis has improved considerably in recent decades.
Typische Symptome: A palpable lump or hardening in the breast; Change in the shape or size of the breast; Dimpling or skin changes (›orange-peel skin‹) on the breast; Discharge from the nipple outside of breastfeeding; Redness or scaling around the nipple; Palpable lymph nodes in the armpit; Persistent pain in a localized area of the breast
Notfall-Hinweis: Any newly felt lump, any sudden change in the breast, or nipple discharge should be checked by a doctor promptly – even though the large majority of such findings turn out to be benign. In someone already diagnosed: severe shortness of breath, unexplained significant weight loss, or new bone pain should be evaluated by a doctor without delay.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Unlike the other conditions in this compass, breast cancer is explicitly not addressed here in terms of a direct psychological contribution to its cause. Breast cancer arises from a complex interplay of genetic predisposition, hormones, cellular aging, and chance – it is not directly connected to a person's personality or subtype, and no single behavior and no single emotional state ›produces‹ this disease on its own. Prostate Cancer (Psychosomatik-Register · Oncology)
The most common cancer in men – usually slow-growing, but often experienced in silence.
Definition: Prostate cancer is the most common malignant tumor in men in Western industrialized nations and arises from uncontrolled cell growth in the prostate, usually in the outer glandular tissue. In most cases it grows very slowly and often remains confined to the prostate for years, though more aggressive forms can spread to bones and lymph nodes. Known risk factors include increasing age, family history, certain genetic changes, and possibly diet and lifestyle – but the exact cause is multifactorial and, for most people affected, cannot be traced to a single origin. Because many courses progress very slowly, low-risk cases are often managed with active surveillance instead of immediate treatment, while more aggressive forms require surgery, radiation, or hormone therapy.
Typische Symptome: Frequent urination, especially at night; Weak or interrupted urine stream; Pain or burning during urination; Blood in urine or semen; Erectile dysfunction; Pain in the lower back, pelvis, or thigh in advanced disease; Unintended weight loss in advanced stages
Notfall-Hinweis: Persistent urinary symptoms, blood in urine or semen, and unexplained bone pain should be evaluated by a urologist promptly – acute urinary retention (being unable to pass urine at all) is an emergency and requires immediate medical care.

Colorectal Cancer (Psychosomatik-Register · Oncology)
One of the most common tumors in Western industrialized nations – and burdened with more shame than almost any other cancer.
Definition: Colorectal cancer is one of the most common malignant tumors in Western industrialized nations and usually arises from initially benign polyps in the lining of the bowel, which can develop into malignant cells over the course of years. The colon and rectum are most commonly affected. Known risk factors include age, genetic predisposition (such as familial adenomatous polyposis or Lynch syndrome), chronic inflammatory bowel disease, a low-fiber diet, lack of exercise, smoking, and alcohol consumption – but the cause is always multifactorial and, for any individual affected, cannot be traced to one specific origin. Because colorectal cancer usually develops slowly from precursor lesions, regular screening colonoscopy demonstrably lowers the risk of disease, since polyps can be removed before they turn malignant.
Typische Symptome: Change in bowel habits lasting several weeks (diarrhea, constipation, or alternating); Blood in the stool or unusually dark, tarry stool; Unexplained abdominal pain or cramping; Unintended weight loss; Persistent fatigue from anemia; A sense of incomplete bowel emptying; A palpable hardening in the abdomen
Notfall-Hinweis: Blood in the stool, persistent changes in bowel habits lasting more than two to three weeks, or unexplained weight loss should be evaluated by a doctor promptly. Sudden, severe abdominal pain with a rigid abdomen, vomiting of stool, or no passage of stool or gas for over 24 hours can indicate a bowel obstruction and require immediate emergency treatment.

Lung Cancer (Psychosomatik-Register · Oncology)
One of the most aggressive cancers, often detected late – and frequently accompanied by unfair blame.
Definition: Lung cancer arises from the uncontrolled proliferation of malignant cells in lung tissue or the bronchi and is among the most common and aggressive cancers. A distinction is made mainly between small-cell and non-small-cell lung cancer, which differ considerably in growth rate and treatment response. Smoking is by far the most significant known risk factor; other contributors include occupational exposure to hazardous substances (such as asbestos or fine particulate matter), radon exposure in homes, genetic predisposition, and – for a meaningful proportion of those affected – none of the known risk factors at all: people who have never smoked also develop lung cancer. Because the disease often only causes noticeable symptoms late, it is frequently discovered at an advanced stage, which complicates diagnosis and treatment.
Typische Symptome: A persistent, changing cough over several weeks; Blood-tinged sputum; Increasing shortness of breath, even with mild exertion; Persistent chest pain, sometimes worse with breathing; Unintended weight loss and loss of appetite; Recurring pneumonia in the same area of the lung; Persistent hoarseness or exhaustion
Notfall-Hinweis: Blood in the sputum, new or worsening shortness of breath, a cough changing over weeks, or unexplained weight loss should be evaluated by a doctor promptly. Call emergency services immediately for sudden severe shortness of breath or coughing up significant amounts of blood.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
With lung cancer especially, this compass takes particular care to rule out any notion of psychological or character-related contribution to its cause – the disease has clearly identified biological and toxicological causes, above all smoking, but also environmental factors, occupation, and genetics, and for some of those affected, no identifiable external cause at all – no character trait is directly connected to it. A person who develops lung cancer bears no character-related blame for it, whether or not they smoked – the social blame that people with this illness so often encounter is not medically supportable and is deliberately not repeated here. What does show up in a subtype-specific way instead is how each person handles an illness that directly affects the breath – the very symbol of being alive – possible stigmatization from those around them, an often late and therefore especially shattering diagnosis, and the question of to whom fear and breathlessness are shown. Skin Cancer (Melanoma) (Psychosomatik-Register · Oncology)
The most aggressive form of skin cancer arises from degenerated pigment cells and can spread early – but is highly treatable when caught in time.
Definition: Malignant melanoma is a malignant tumor that develops from the pigment-producing cells of the skin (melanocytes) and, much more rarely, can also occur in mucous membranes or the eye. It is among the more aggressive forms of skin cancer, since compared to the more common, usually slower-growing non-melanoma skin cancers (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), it can spread earlier via the lymphatic and blood vessels to other organs. Recognized risk factors include intense UV exposure and sunburns, especially in childhood, a fair skin type, a high number of moles, genetic predisposition, and a weakened immune system. Prognosis depends decisively on tumor thickness and stage at diagnosis – when caught early, cure rates are very high, which is why early detection through regular skin checks is of central importance.
Typische Symptome: A newly appearing or changing mole (asymmetry, irregular border, multiple colors, diameter over 5 mm, raised surface – the ABCDE rule); Itching, bleeding, or oozing of a pigmented spot; A spot that clearly differs from the surrounding moles (the ›ugly duckling‹ sign); New dark streaks under finger- or toenails; Swollen, hardened lymph nodes near a suspicious spot; A pigmented spot that does not heal; Unexplained lumps under the skin in someone with a known melanoma
Notfall-Hinweis: Have any new or changing mole evaluated by a dermatologist promptly; for a known melanoma with newly appearing lumps, severe headaches, breathing difficulties, or unexplained weight loss, seek medical attention immediately.

How is a changed mole talked about – with a doctor, a partner, at all? And how does the relationship to one's own visible body change when a scar, a wound, or a treatment alters it permanently? Stomach Cancer (Psychosomatik-Register · Oncology)
A malignant tumor of the stomach lining that causes hardly any symptoms for a long time and is often discovered late.
Definition: Stomach cancer (gastric carcinoma) most often develops from the cells of the stomach lining, in the vast majority of cases as what is called an adenocarcinoma. Known risk factors include chronic infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, certain dietary habits (heavily salted, smoked, or cured foods), smoking, high alcohol consumption, pre-existing damage to the stomach lining such as chronic gastritis or stomach polyps, and a family predisposition. In its early stages, the disease often runs without clear symptoms, which is why it is frequently diagnosed only at an advanced stage, once the tumor has already penetrated the stomach wall or spread to nearby lymph nodes or organs. Treatment depends on stage and spread and, depending on the findings, includes surgery, chemotherapy, and in certain cases further systemic therapies.
Typische Symptome: Persistent feeling of fullness or pressure in the upper abdomen, even after small meals; Loss of appetite and aversion to certain foods, especially meat; Unintentional weight loss; Nausea and recurring vomiting, sometimes with blood; Black-colored stool as a sign of internal bleeding; Increasing difficulty swallowing with tumors near the stomach entrance; Persistent fatigue and paleness from chronic blood loss
Notfall-Hinweis: Seek prompt medical evaluation for persistent unexplained weight loss, blood in vomit or black stool, severe difficulty swallowing, or a palpable hardening in the upper abdomen.

Pancreatic Cancer (Psychosomatik-Register · Oncology)
A tumor of the pancreas that causes hardly any symptoms for a long time and is therefore often discovered late.
Definition: Pancreatic cancer (pancreatic carcinoma) most often develops from the cells lining the ducts of the exocrine gland tissue and is among the cancers with a particularly unfavorable prognosis, since the pancreas lies deep in the abdomen and tumors there cause no clear symptoms for a long time. Known risk factors include smoking, chronic alcohol use, an already existing chronic pancreatitis, newly developed diabetes mellitus at an older age, significant obesity, and certain familial and genetic predispositions. Because the gland produces both digestive enzymes and insulin, a tumor can, depending on its location, impair both digestion and blood sugar metabolism. Treatment ranges, depending on stage, from surgical removal followed by chemotherapy to purely systemic or palliative approaches when surgery is no longer possible.
Typische Symptome: Upper abdominal pain that often radiates in a belt-like pattern into the back; Yellowing of skin and eyes (jaundice) from bile duct obstruction; Unexplained, often rapid weight loss; Newly appearing or suddenly worsening diabetes mellitus; Loss of appetite and nausea; Pale, greasy-looking stool and dark urine; Persistent fatigue with no obvious cause
Notfall-Hinweis: Seek prompt medical evaluation for sudden yellowing of skin or eyes, severe persistent upper abdominal or back pain, or rapidly progressing unexplained weight loss.

Leukemia (Psychosomatik-Register · Oncology)
Cancers of the white blood cells that arise in the bone marrow and crowd out normal blood formation.
Definition: Leukemia is an umbrella term for various malignant diseases of the blood-forming system, in which immature or improperly matured white blood cells multiply uncontrollably in the bone marrow and crowd out normal blood formation. A broad distinction is made between acute forms, which progress rapidly and require immediate treatment, and chronic forms, which often develop slowly over years, as well as between myeloid and lymphocytic leukemias depending on the affected cell line. The exact causes are usually multifactorial and include genetic changes in the blood-forming cells, ionizing radiation, certain chemicals such as benzene, prior chemotherapy, and, in rarer cases, hereditary predisposition. Treatment ranges, depending on type and stage, from chemotherapy to targeted medications and immunotherapy to stem cell transplantation, often involving longer phases of intensive treatment and a weakened immune defense.
Typische Symptome: Persistent, unusually strong fatigue and reduced stamina; Paleness from anemia; Increased susceptibility to infections due to a lack of functioning white blood cells; A tendency to bruise easily and pinpoint skin bleeding; Increased bleeding from gums or nose; Pain in bones or joints; Swollen, usually painless lymph nodes and night sweats
Notfall-Hinweis: Seek prompt medical evaluation for high fever combined with severe exhaustion, unusual bleeding, marked paleness, or rapidly increasing lymph node swelling.

Chronic Kidney Disease (Psychosomatik-Register · Kidney & Bladder)
A quiet, years-long progressive loss of kidney function that causes barely any symptoms for a long time.
Definition: Chronic kidney disease refers to a progressive, usually irreversible loss of the kidneys' filtering function over months to years. The most common causes are diabetes mellitus and high blood pressure, alongside chronic kidney inflammation, congenital malformations, polycystic kidney disease, or long-term misuse of certain painkillers. The disease is classified into five stages, ranging from mildly reduced to fully lost function, at which point dialysis or transplantation becomes necessary. Because the kidneys can compensate for a considerable loss of function over a long time, the disease often goes unnoticed until an advanced stage and is frequently discovered by chance during routine checkups.
Typische Symptome: Persistent fatigue and weakness; Fluid retention in the legs, ankles, or eyelids; Foamy or changed urine; Hard-to-control high blood pressure; Itchy skin; Loss of appetite and nausea; Frequent nighttime urination

Erectile Dysfunction (Psychosomatik-Register · Other Conditions)
A widespread, often shame-laden dysfunction with mostly organic causes – and a well-documented stress component.
Definition: Erectile dysfunction refers to the repeated inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfying intercourse. It is widespread and becomes more common with age, but can affect men of any age. The most common causes are organic: circulatory problems from arteriosclerosis, diabetes, high blood pressure, hormonal changes, neurological conditions, and side effects of numerous medications, for instance for high blood pressure or depression. Alongside this, a psychological component is well documented: performance pressure, fear of failure, and general stress can worsen an existing dysfunction or – especially in younger men – trigger erectile difficulties even without an underlying organic condition, often in a self-reinforcing cycle of worry and renewed failure to achieve an erection. In many cases, organic and psychological factors interact.
Typische Symptome: Difficulty achieving an erection; Difficulty maintaining an erection; Diminishing nighttime or morning spontaneous erections; Reduced sexual desire as an accompanying symptom; Tension or avoidance behavior before intimate situations; Withdrawal from the partnership around sexuality; Strain on self-esteem
Notfall-Hinweis: A painful erection lasting several hours (priapism) is a medical emergency and requires immediate treatment. If the dysfunction appears suddenly together with chest pain or shortness of breath, this can indicate a cardiovascular condition and should be evaluated promptly.

Unfulfilled Desire to Have Children (Psychosomatik-Register · Other Conditions)
A deeply burdensome life situation with diverse medical causes on both sides – not a matter of character.
Definition: An unfulfilled desire to have children is usually diagnosed when no pregnancy occurs after about a year of regular, unprotected intercourse. The causes are roughly split evenly between factors on the woman's side (such as fallopian tube problems, endometriosis, hormonal disorders, declining egg quality with age) and the man's side (such as reduced sperm quality or count), and a combination of several factors on both sides is common. In a relevant share of couples, depending on the study between 15 and 30 percent, no clear cause can be identified despite extensive diagnostics – this is referred to as idiopathic or unexplained infertility. An unfulfilled desire to have children is therefore, as a rule, a multifactorial medical situation, not the result of a particular psychological pattern, even though the monthly recurring disappointment itself can generate considerable emotional stress.
Typische Symptome: Recurring disappointment with every missed period; Growing tension around ovulation and the timing of intercourse; Diminishing spontaneity in sexuality due to ›scheduled sex‹; Exhaustion from hormone treatments and repeated diagnostics; Withdrawal from social circles, especially around pregnancies nearby; Tension and differing coping paces within the partnership; Feelings of shame, isolation, or failure despite no fault of one's own
Notfall-Hinweis: If pregnancy does not occur after about a year (after six months for women over 35), specialist evaluation is advisable. In cases of persistent severe exhaustion, depressive mood, or growing strain on the relationship, psychotherapeutic or couples counseling can offer relief.
Every person can be affected by an unfulfilled desire to have children, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings about the emotional experience of this situation – no psychological pattern causes infertility, and this text never replaces specialist medical or reproductive medicine evaluation.
Explicitly upfront: an unfulfilled desire to have children usually has physical, often multifactorial causes on both sides of a partnership, or no identifiable cause at all – not a particular psychological pattern that would need to be ›resolved‹ for a pregnancy to occur. Such a notion would not only be medically wrong, but additionally hurtful for those affected, who already hear often enough that they should ›just relax more‹. What this is about instead is the very real emotional experience of a situation that accompanies many couples for months or years: the monthly swing between hope and disappointment, coping with treatments and diagnostics, the question of who grief gets shown to, and comparison with a social circle in which pregnancies seem to happen effortlessly. Each of the 27 subtypes shows its own pattern in handling this particular form of recurring disappointment.

Periodontitis (Psychosomatik-Register · Other Conditions)
A chronic inflammation of the tooth-supporting structures that gradually breaks down gum tissue and jawbone.
Definition: Periodontitis is a chronic, bacterially triggered inflammation of the tooth-supporting structures that, left untreated, can lead to progressive breakdown of gum tissue, connective tissue, and jawbone, up to tooth loss. It is caused by a bacterial biofilm (plaque) at the gumline, to which the immune system responds with an inflammatory reaction that, given the right predisposition, poor oral hygiene, smoking, diabetes, or chronic stress, takes on a life of its own and increasingly attacks surrounding tissue instead of containing it. The disease usually progresses over years, quietly and largely without pain, which is why it is often only noticed once significant bone loss or loosened teeth are already present. It is now considered established that chronic inflammation in the mouth is also linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and poorer diabetes control.
Typische Symptome: Bleeding gums when brushing; Red, swollen gums; Receding gums and exposed tooth necks; Persistent bad breath; Increasing looseness of individual teeth; Discharge of fluid or pus at the gumline; Changes in bite from shifting teeth
Notfall-Hinweis: Have severely swollen, painful gums with fever or noticeable tooth looseness evaluated by a dentist promptly; persistent bleeding gums should not be put off even without acute pain.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
In Traditional Chinese Medicine, the Stomach meridian runs directly through the gums of the upper jaw, which is why chronic gum inflammation there is often associated with long-suppressed ›stomach fire‹ – something boiling internally that isn't allowed to surface. The mouth is also the first boundary between inside and outside, the place where it is literally decided what gets let in and what gets rejected, and where, figuratively, one ›bites down‹ or ›grits one's teeth‹. Psychosomatically, periodontitis is therefore often read as a picture of chronically held-back anger or permanently overextended self-control, settling as quiet inflammation right at this boundary. Chronic Cystitis (Bladder Infection) (Psychosomatik-Register · Kidney & Bladder)
A repeatedly recurring inflammation of the bladder lining that often becomes a lasting theme far beyond the single acute infection – with burning, a sense of pressure, and constant worry about the next flare-up.
Definition: Cystitis is an inflammation of the bladder lining, most often caused by ascending bacteria, in the vast majority of cases Escherichia coli from the person's own gut. Chronic or recurrent cystitis is diagnosed when at least two infections occur within six months, or three within a year. Women are affected considerably more often than men because of their shorter urethra. Contributing factors include sexual intercourse, hormonal changes such as menopause, a weakened local immune environment of the mucosa, habitually holding in the urge to urinate, and in some cases anatomical particularities. In some sufferers, typical complaints appear without a sufficient bacterial count in the urine – this is then called interstitial or non-bacterial irritable bladder syndrome, a closely related but distinct condition.

Notfall-Hinweis: For flank pain, high fever, chills, or a strong sense of being seriously unwell, seek prompt medical evaluation – this can indicate an ascending kidney infection that requires treatment.

Glaucoma (Psychosomatik-Register · Eyes)
A gradually progressing disease of the optic nerve, usually caused by elevated intraocular pressure, that slowly and often imperceptibly narrows the field of vision – until a considerable part is already lost.
Definition: Glaucoma refers to a group of eye diseases in which the optic nerve is progressively damaged, most often as a result of elevated intraocular pressure caused by a disturbed drainage balance of the aqueous humor. What makes glaucoma treacherous is its gradual course: the visual field first narrows from the outside inward, without those affected noticing this in everyday life, since the brain compensates for the emerging gaps for a long time. Left untreated, glaucoma can lead to complete blindness. Risk factors include family history, older age, nearsightedness, diabetes, and generally elevated intraocular pressure. Regular ophthalmologic check-ups are crucial, since the resulting optic nerve damage cannot be reversed – treatment aims to halt further progression.
Typische Symptome: Gradual, usually unnoticed loss of the outer visual field; Occasional visual disturbances or the perception of halos around light sources; A sense of pressure in the eye, more rarely headache; In an acute glaucoma attack: sudden severe eye pain with nausea; Reddened, hardened eye during an acute attack; Poorer vision at dusk; Increasing stumbling due to a restricted field of vision
Notfall-Hinweis: For sudden, severe eye pain with a reddened, hardened eye, worsening vision, and nausea, seek emergency ophthalmologic care immediately – suspected acute glaucoma attack, which can lead to blindness within a few hours.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.

Psychosomatically, the gradually narrowing visual field of glaucoma often reads as an image of a viewpoint that has unconsciously narrowed over years – where breadth of vision and openness to the future increasingly give way to a rigid focus on what is immediately necessary. Endometriosis (Psychosomatik-Register · Other Conditions)
A chronic inflammatory disease in which tissue resembling the uterine lining grows outside the uterus, often causing severe, recurring pain for years before a diagnosis is even made.
Definition: Endometriosis is a chronic, benign, but often very distressing disease in which tissue resembling the uterine lining grows outside the uterine cavity – for instance on the ovaries, fallopian tubes, peritoneum, or more rarely on other organs. This tissue responds to the monthly hormonal cycle just like the uterine lining itself, but unlike it cannot drain through the vagina, which leads to inflammatory reactions, scarring, and adhesions. Those affected very often experience severe menstrual pain, chronic pelvic pain, and fertility problems. A particularly serious and well-documented problem is the diagnostic delay: on average, several years pass – studies frequently cite six to ten years – between the first symptoms and a confirmed diagnosis, because menstrual pain is often trivialized within the healthcare system for a long time. This delay is not the fault of those affected, but of a structural underestimation of the condition that is by now widely recognized as a problem.
Typische Symptome: Severe, often worsening menstrual pain that goes far beyond normal period discomfort; Chronic pelvic or back pain also outside the period; Pain during intercourse; Pain during urination or bowel movements, especially during menstruation; Unfulfilled desire to have children due to reduced fertility; Heavy, irregular bleeding; Chronic exhaustion from sustained pain and inflammation
Notfall-Hinweis: For sudden, very severe pelvic pain with circulatory instability, seek prompt medical evaluation to rule out acute causes such as a ruptured cyst. For persistent severe menstrual pain, always seek early gynecological evaluation rather than accepting it as normal.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner. These interpretive offerings are explicitly not a suggestion that the real, often very severe pain of endometriosis is ›only‹ psychologically caused or would disappear through inner work alone – the physical illness is real, must be taken seriously, and belongs in medical and, where necessary, surgical treatment.
Endometriosis is first and foremost a real, often long-underestimated physical illness whose pain is not imagined and not ›just in the head‹ – stating this up front matters more here than any interpretation. Psychosomatically – without downplaying the physical severity – one can additionally ask what pattern shows itself when a person's own body sends recurring, unmistakable pain signals for years while those around her fail to take it seriously for a long time. Bladder Weakness / Incontinence (Psychosomatik-Register · Kidney & Bladder)
An involuntary loss of control over the bladder that occurs far more often than it is openly talked about – from slight leaking when coughing to a complete loss of control.
Definition: Urinary incontinence refers to any involuntary loss of urine. Several forms are distinguished: stress incontinence shows up during physical exertion, coughing, sneezing, or laughing and usually results from a weakened pelvic floor, often after childbirth or during menopause due to hormonal changes. Urge incontinence comes with a sudden, barely suppressible urge to urinate, often caused by an overactive bladder. Other causes can include neurological diseases, prostate conditions in men, certain surgeries, or age-related tissue changes. Incontinence is not rare and not a sign of personal failure – estimates suggest millions of people of all ages are affected, with a considerable share of cases, out of shame, never medically evaluated at all, even though good treatment options exist, ranging from pelvic floor training to medication to surgical procedures.
Typische Symptome: Involuntary loss of urine when coughing, sneezing, laughing, or during physical exertion; Sudden, barely controllable urge to urinate; Frequent nighttime urination; Feeling of never being able to fully empty the bladder; Difficulty reaching the toilet in time; Skin irritation in the intimate area from ongoing moisture; Social withdrawal out of worry about visible accidents
Notfall-Hinweis: For sudden-onset incontinence combined with numbness, signs of paralysis, or severe back pain, seek prompt medical evaluation – possible sign of a neurological emergency.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner. Incontinence is a physical functional disorder, not a reason for shame.

Psychosomatically, incontinence often reads as an image of having to let go without having chosen to – a loss of control over a bodily function that, for many people, is closely tied to dignity and self-determination. Kidney Stones (Psychosomatik-Register · Kidney & Bladder)
Solid deposits in the urinary tract that, when they pass, can cause some of the most intense pain the body can produce.
Definition: Kidney stones (nephrolithiasis) form when minerals dissolved in the urine, such as calcium, oxalate, uric acid, or phosphate, crystallize into solid deposits. Contributing factors include insufficient fluid intake, certain dietary habits, metabolic disorders, recurrent urinary tract infections, and family history. Small stones are often passed unnoticed, while larger ones can obstruct the ureter or renal pelvis, triggering a wave-like, severe flank pain known as renal colic that frequently radiates into the groin. Treatment ranges from generous fluid intake and pain management to shock-wave lithotripsy or surgical removal for larger, lodged stones.
Typische Symptome: Sudden, wave-like flank pain; Pain radiating into the groin or lower abdomen; Blood in the urine; Nausea and vomiting during the colic; Frequent urge to urinate with little urine passed; Burning during urination; Restless shifting of position during the pain attack
Notfall-Hinweis: Seek an emergency room immediately for fever combined with flank pain, a complete absence of urine output, uncontrollable vomiting, or extremely severe pain that does not respond to painkillers – these can indicate an obstructed infection or impending kidney damage.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
In Traditional Chinese Medicine, the kidneys are considered the seat of the deepest life reserves and closely tied to the water element and the emotion of fear – a stone forming there can often be read psychosomatically as an image of inner material that has hardened over a long time without flowing: worries, demands, or feelings that were never voiced and therefore never released, but instead slowly compacted until they announce themselves painfully. Subtype-specific patterns emerge above all in what someone holds back over the years, how suddenly erupting, barely controllable pain is experienced, and how the loss of control during the colic itself is handled. Each of the 27 subtypes shows its own pattern.
--- Typ 1: Hardened standards ---
SE1: Over the years, the self-preservation One holds back unspoken irritation about small inaccuracies in daily life instead of voicing it – this steady holding-back can psychosomatically compact into something that eventually breaks through painfully.
SO1: The social One consistently puts her own needs behind what seems right for the community, and usually swallows resentment about situations felt as unjust long before she even notices it.
SX1: When a sudden colic strikes, the sexual One's anger comes out loud and immediate, aimed straight at doctors and family, instead of the disciplined restraint other One variants tend to favor.
--- Typ 2: Withheld demands ---
SE2: Own wishes are rarely stated directly by the self-preservation Two, who prefers to quietly arrange for her needs to be met indirectly – when that fails over the years, a resentment builds up beneath the surface that she herself barely notices.
SO2: Within her wide circle of acquaintances, the social Two often reports sudden colic pain only late, out of fear that an acute emergency might distract others from their own concerns.
SX2: Her fear during the colic is confessed openly by the sexual Two to the one important person, rather than continuing to be there for others while the pain still lasts, unlike other Two variants.
--- Typ 3: No room for downtime ---
SE3: An acute colic forces the self-preservation Three into a pause she otherwise rarely allows herself – her first impulse is usually to become functional again as quickly as possible, rather than taking the cause seriously.
SO3: Outwardly, the social Three tends to downplay the severity of the pain attack so as not to jeopardize her image of resilience, sometimes returning to her schedule too soon.
SX3: Her otherwise flawless facade gets dropped by the sexual Three during the colic, at least in front of the one important person, where she shows genuine exhaustion she otherwise consistently hides.

SX4: The pain gets described intensely by the sexual Four to the one person she feels bonded to, rather than processing it more inwardly like other Four variants.

Acute Kidney Failure (Psychosomatik-Register · Kidney & Bladder)
A sudden, often dramatic collapse of kidney function within hours to days that requires immediate treatment.
Definition: Acute kidney failure (acute kidney injury) is a rapid loss of kidney function occurring within hours to a few days. The causes are varied: insufficient blood flow to the kidneys due to severe fluid loss, hemorrhage, or circulatory shock (prerenal); direct damage to kidney tissue from medications, contrast agents, toxins, or inflammation (renal); or an obstruction of the urinary tract, for example from stones or an enlarged prostate (postrenal). Acute kidney failure often develops in the context of a severe underlying condition, such as sepsis, major surgery, or as a worsening of pre-existing chronic kidney disease. Unlike the chronic form, acute kidney failure is often reversible if the triggering cause is treated promptly, but it can quickly become life-threatening if left untreated.
Typische Symptome: Markedly reduced or absent urine output; Rapid fluid retention in the legs, face, or lungs; Sudden confusion or drowsiness; Nausea and vomiting; Shortness of breath; Cardiac arrhythmias from disrupted electrolyte levels; Pronounced, rapidly setting-in fatigue
Notfall-Hinweis: Acute kidney failure is always a medical emergency and requires immediate medical treatment, usually in a hospital. Call emergency services without delay for severely reduced or absent urine output, shortness of breath, confusion, or cardiac arrhythmias – every delay can worsen the kidneys' chances of recovery.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Unlike chronic kidney disease, acute kidney failure usually strikes unprepared and suddenly – often in the context of an already severe situation such as surgery, an infection, or shock. Its causes are organic and situational, not rooted in character. What is psychosomatically interesting is therefore less a possible contribution to its cause than the way the abrupt loss of control over one's own body is handled in the middle of an already stressful situation: How does someone react to a sudden medical emergency? How much trust is placed in the treatment team at a moment when swift action outweighs one's own resources? And how is the uncertainty over whether kidney function will recover handled? Each of the 27 subtypes shows its own pattern in dealing with this abrupt crisis.
--- Typ 1: Composure in the acute situation ---
SE1: In the acute crisis, the self-preservation One tries to keep functioning in a structured way despite the exceptional situation, and afterward often blames herself over whether an earlier warning sign was missed.
SO1: Toward the treatment team, the social One appears mostly cooperative and matter-of-fact even in the acute situation, while largely holding back her own fear of the uncertainty.
SX1: Fear and anger during a sudden crisis are not held back by the sexual One – they go straight to nursing staff and family, unlike the quieter containment other One variants tend to favor.
--- Typ 2: Worrying about others in the middle of her own crisis ---
SE2: Even from the hospital bed, the self-preservation Two often worries first about who will take over everyday tasks at home, instead of fully focusing on her own acute treatment.
SO2: Even from the hospital bed, the social Two quickly reassures visitors and family that she is already doing better, in order to spare them her own worry.
SX2: In the acute situation, the sexual Two exceptionally allows the one important person to take care of her, instead of immediately returning to caregiving like other Two variants.
--- Typ 3: The breakdown that must not happen ---
SE3: From her hospital bed, the self-preservation Three often tries to keep answering work messages, because a complete standstill feels almost unbearable to her.
SO3: Toward colleagues and superiors, the social Three often frames the acute crisis in strikingly matter-of-fact terms, almost like an organizational detail, so as not to jeopardize her image of resilience.
SX3: Genuinely dropping her otherwise flawless self-presentation happens for the sexual Three only in front of the one important person, in the middle of the acute crisis, where real fear shows.
--- Typ 4: A crisis that stirs up everything at once ---
SE4: In an acute crisis, fear tends to get pushed down and handled functionally by the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, rather than expressed – a marked departure from the way her type is otherwise known for airing feelings.
SO4: In the abrupt severity of the situation, the social Four occasionally finds a painful confirmation that life runs especially hard for her, instead of classifying it as a temporary medical episode.

Pyelonephritis (Psychosomatik-Register · Kidney & Bladder)
A usually bacterial infection of the renal pelvis that develops from an ascending bladder infection and progresses rapidly with fever.
Definition: Pyelonephritis is a usually bacterial infection of the renal pelvis and adjacent kidney tissue that typically develops when pathogens ascend from the bladder through the ureters. It is favored by obstructions to urine flow, for example from stones or an enlarged prostate, as well as by pregnancy, diabetes mellitus, or a weakened immune system. Unlike a simple urinary tract infection, pyelonephritis typically comes with high fever, chills, and a marked feeling of illness, and must be treated with antibiotics to prevent the infection from spreading into the bloodstream (urosepsis) or causing lasting kidney damage. With timely treatment it usually heals without lasting effects; left untreated or with repeated episodes, it can permanently damage kidney tissue.
Typische Symptome: High fever with chills; One- or two-sided flank pain; Tenderness to percussion over the affected kidney; Burning during urination; Frequent urge to urinate; Cloudy, foul-smelling urine; Pronounced general feeling of illness and exhaustion
Notfall-Hinweis: Prompt medical treatment should follow for high fever with chills and flank pain. If confusion, very low blood pressure, a racing heart, or rapidly increasing circulatory instability appear as well, life-threatening urosepsis may be developing – seek an emergency room immediately in that case.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Pyelonephritis usually develops because an initially harmless-seeming bladder infection, left untreated or underestimated, keeps ascending until it reaches the more sensitive kidney tissue. Psychosomatically, this course can often be read as an image of how the body's first, still quiet warning signals are handled – whether they are taken seriously and treated early, or only get attention once high fever and clear pain leave no way around them. In Traditional Chinese Medicine, the kidneys are also closely tied to willpower and the body's deepest reserves, so an inflammation at this site can also be read as an acute assault on exactly this foundational stability. Each of the 27 subtypes shows its own pattern in dealing with early warning signs, acute illness, and the need to genuinely hold back for the duration of treatment.
--- Typ 1: Pushing through despite the fever ---
SE1: The self-preservation One initially treats early signs of a bladder infection with her own tried-and-tested home remedies and disciplined perseverance, until the high fever of the ascending infection forces her to see a doctor.
SO1: Even with high fever, the social One initially tries to keep meeting her obligations toward family or colleagues, out of concern about burdening others through her absence.
SX1: A sudden, painful worsening triggers anger that the sexual One directs straight at doctors, skipping past the composed self-control other One variants tend to favor.
--- Typ 2: Taking care of herself last ---
SE2: Despite high fever, the self-preservation Two initially tries to keep the household running instead of lying down and seeking medical help early enough.
SO2: Within her circle, the social Two often mentions her own feverish illness only in passing, while continuing to ask about others' worries.
SX2: During the high fever, the sexual Two genuinely lets the one important person take care of her, instead of taking on the caregiving role herself as usual.
--- Typ 3: Keeping going despite feeling ill ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three often ignores early symptoms of a urinary tract infection as long as she still functions, only seeking medical help once the high fever and flank pain arrive.
SO3: Outwardly, the social Three often wants to keep the severity of the infection as minimal as possible, to keep appearing capable, and sometimes returns to her schedule too soon.
SX3: During the high fever, the sexual Three genuinely shows exhaustion, but only in front of the one important person – otherwise she keeps her flawless facade consistently intact.
--- Typ 4: Illness as a tangible confirmation ---
SE4: General malaise is mostly shouldered in silence by the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, with little complaint rather than voiced – behavior that clearly contradicts the dramatic expression typical of her type.
SO4: In the sudden severity of the feverish illness, the social Four occasionally finds a painful confirmation of how vulnerable and unprotected she already feels.
SX4: Her fear during the high fever gets shared intensely by the sexual Four with the one person she feels bonded to, rather than withdrawing.

Kidney Cancer (Psychosomatik-Register · Kidney & Bladder)
A malignant kidney tumor that typically occurs later in life, causes no symptoms for a long time, and is often discovered by chance.
Definition: Kidney cancer (most commonly renal cell carcinoma) is a malignant tumor arising from kidney tissue. Recognized risk factors include smoking, obesity, high blood pressure, long-term dialysis treatment with acquired kidney cysts, and certain genetic predispositions, such as von Hippel–Lindau syndrome. The risk of disease increases with age, and men are affected somewhat more often than women. Because the kidney can compensate for a long time and the tumor itself often causes no pain, kidney cancer is frequently discovered by chance during imaging done for another reason, sometimes only at an advanced stage. Depending on the stage, treatment ranges from partial or complete surgical removal of the kidney, to targeted drugs and immunotherapies, to a combination of these approaches; the prognosis depends decisively on the stage at diagnosis.
Typische Symptome: Blood in the urine; Persistent, dull flank pain; A palpable mass or swelling in the abdomen or flank; Unexplained weight loss; Persistent fatigue; Recurring, unexplained fever; High blood pressure or anemia with no other identifiable cause
Notfall-Hinweis: Blood in the urine, a palpable lump in the flank area, or unexplained weight loss should be evaluated by a doctor promptly. For known kidney cancer with severe flank pain, pronounced shortness of breath, bone pain, or neurological deficits, seek medical help immediately.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
As with all oncological conditions in this compass, it explicitly holds true here too: psychological patterns do not cause cancer. Kidney cancer develops through an interplay of biological factors – smoking, obesity, high blood pressure, genetic predispositions such as von Hippel–Lindau syndrome, long-term dialysis treatment, age, and simple chance – none of which are directly connected to a person's personality. Anyone who receives this diagnosis carries no character-based blame for it. What follows instead concerns something different: how differently people react to the diagnosis depending on subtype, how they talk about it with doctors and family (or don't), how they experience the loss of control during surgery, possible dialysis, and follow-up care, and how their relationship to their own body changes through treatment and uncertainty. Each of the 27 subtypes shows its own pattern in dealing with diagnosis, treatment, and uncertainty – not in the origin of the illness.
--- Typ 1: Seeking order within uncertainty ---
SE1: After the diagnosis, the self-preservation One initially seeks stability in as precisely structured a treatment plan as possible, while often also blaming herself unnecessarily for not noticing the incidentally discovered tumor sooner.
SO1: The social One tends to talk about her diagnosis with her circle only once she has informed herself fully on the medical side, out of concern about causing unnecessary alarm with half-knowledge.
SX1: The diagnosis itself becomes a target for the sexual One's anger, shown openly and immediately toward doctors and family, rather than the composed restraint other One variants tend to favor.
--- Typ 2: Caregiving that has to reverse ---
SE2: After surgery, the self-preservation Two tries to quickly be there for others again instead of genuinely allowing her own recovery time, often concealing her ongoing exhaustion in the process.
SO2: Telling many people her diagnosis at once, before she has processed it herself, often overwhelms the social Two – she tends to worry more about others' reactions than about her own processing.
SX2: Genuinely letting herself be cared for after the diagnosis, instead of immediately switching back into the giving role, succeeds for the sexual Two at least within the one important relationship – a role reversal that comes easier to her than to other Two variants, yet still remains unfamiliar.
--- Typ 3: Functional despite a missing kidney ---
SE3: After the surgical removal of part or all of a kidney, the self-preservation Three often plans her return to work rushed, in order to show as little loss of performance as possible.
SO3: Despite the diagnosis, the social Three continues to appear capable and composed outwardly, while carefully keeping her exhaustion after surgery out of her public image.
SX3: As soon as she is alone with the one important person, the sexual Three lets her flawless facade drop and shows there the exhaustion she otherwise consistently conceals.

Alzheimer's Disease / Dementia (Psychosomatik-Register · Nervous System & Psyche)
A progressive brain disease in which memory, orientation, and eventually personality itself are lost piece by piece.
Definition: Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia and a progressive neurodegenerative brain disease in which misfolded proteins – beta-amyloid plaques and tau tangles – accumulate in brain tissue, gradually causing nerve cells and their connections to die off. The course usually begins insidiously with short-term memory problems and progresses over years to disorientation, language difficulties, personality changes, and eventually complete loss of independence. There are also other forms of dementia with their own causes, such as vascular dementia, which results from repeated small disruptions in blood flow to the brain and often progresses in steps rather than steadily, as well as mixed forms of both. By far the greatest risk factor is age; genetic predisposition, in rare cases inherited early-onset forms, and vascular risk factors such as high blood pressure, diabetes, or smoking – which particularly favor vascular dementia – add to that risk.
Typische Symptome: Increasing forgetfulness, especially for recent events; Difficulty orienting in time and place; Word-finding difficulties and a shrinking vocabulary; Declining judgment in everyday decisions; Withdrawal from activities and social contact; Mood swings, irritability, or personality changes; Growing loss of the ability to manage daily life independently
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
The most important clarification first: neither Alzheimer's disease nor other forms of dementia arise from a particular personality, an unresolved wound, or a psychological pattern – their causes lie in misfolded proteins accumulating in the brain, in genetic predisposition, in advancing age, and, in the case of vascular dementia, in impaired blood flow through the vessels. No subtype carries a higher risk of developing dementia, and no one is responsible for their own forgetting through character or behavior. What does differ from subtype to subtype is solely how a person copes with the gradual loss of memory, orientation, and eventually a piece of their own identity – how they experience the diagnosis itself while they can still grasp it, how they communicate with family, what role they must renegotiate in their relationships, and how, where necessary, they learn to accept help. This compass describes these different paths of coping – never a cause.
--- Typ 1: When the inner yardstick blurs ---
SE1: The self-preservation One clings to clear routines and a fixed daily structure for as long as possible even after the first memory lapses, often with notes, lists, and rituals that compensate for what is gradually becoming harder. This strategy helps for a while, but it can mask the real fear of losing control instead of addressing it openly with family.
SO1: Having carried responsibility for others for years, the social One finds it especially painful to become increasingly dependent on outside care herself. If she is told early and respectfully what is happening medically, she can more easily make peace with her new role instead of fighting it.
SX1: The sexual One expresses her feelings more directly than other One variants, and frustration over her own forgetting shows itself more immediately in her rather than staying hidden. This more open expression can, paradoxically, help family members recognize earlier where support is needed.
--- Typ 2: When giving turns into receiving ---
SE2: Caring for others came naturally to the self-preservation Two for decades; now being cared for herself can initially feel like the loss of her own role. Family members who continue to leave her small tasks she can still feel useful doing often noticeably ease this transition.
SO2: The social Two often built her identity on knowing she was important and indispensable to many people. As this web of connections fades with declining memory, it often hits her harder than the memory loss itself.
SX2: In her closest relationship, the sexual Two was already more willing to engage in mutual care rather than give exclusively. This earlier openness to closeness and dependency can make it easier for her to accept care from exactly this one person as the illness progresses.
--- Typ 3: When the success story dissolves ---
SE3: Her practical competence in everyday life was proof of her own ability to the self-preservation Three for years; the first mistakes in familiar tasks are therefore often experienced by her as shameful, and she initially hides them from her own family.
SO3: Professional and social success often shaped the social Three's self-image for de …

Parkinson's Disease (Psychosomatik-Register · Nervous System & Psyche)
A progressive disease of the nervous system in which the loss of dopamine-producing cells increasingly slows, stiffens, and causes involuntary trembling in movement.
Definition: Parkinson's disease is a chronic, progressive neurodegenerative disease in which nerve cells that produce the neurotransmitter dopamine gradually die off in a specific area of the midbrain, the substantia nigra. The resulting dopamine deficiency leads to the classic motor core symptoms – resting tremor, muscle stiffness (rigidity), slowed movement (bradykinesia), and postural instability – as well as frequent non-motor accompanying symptoms such as impaired sense of smell, sleep disturbances, constipation, or depressive moods, which can precede the movement disorder by years in some cases. The exact cause remains unclear for most of those affected; it is thought to involve an interplay of genetic predisposition, aging processes in the nervous system, and possible environmental factors such as exposure to certain pesticides, with only a small proportion of cases traceable to clearly hereditary genetic changes.
Typische Symptome: Resting tremor, usually starting in one hand; Slowed, short-stepped movements (bradykinesia); Increased muscle tension and stiffness (rigidity); Increasingly stooped posture and gait and balance problems; Mask-like, less expressive facial expression; Quieter, more monotone speech; Non-motor accompanying symptoms such as loss of smell, sleep disturbances, or depressive mood
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Here too, the decisive clarification comes first: Parkinson's disease does not arise from a particular personality or a psychological pattern, but from the progressive death of dopamine-producing nerve cells in the midbrain – favored by genetic predisposition, the natural aging process of the nervous system, and, in a smaller proportion of cases, environmental influences. No subtype falls ill more often, less often, or more severely, and no one is responsible for their own trembling through behavior or character. What differs among the 27 subtypes is solely how a person deals with the progressive restriction of their freedom of movement, with visible symptoms in public, with growing dependence on help, and with the questions such a diagnosis raises about their own identity. This section describes exactly these different paths of coping – never a cause.
--- Typ 1: When the hand no longer obeys ---
SE1: Precise, controlled movements mattered to the self-preservation One in everyday life; she usually corrected any inaccuracy immediately. A tremor she cannot stop no matter how hard she tries therefore confronts her directly with the limits of her otherwise so reliable self-control.
SO1: The social One wanted to be seen by those around her as a reliable, functioning role model; visible motor symptoms in public contradict this self-image, which is why she often tries at first to conceal them for as long as possible.
SX1: The sexual One discharges inner tension more immediately than other One variants, rather than suppressing it permanently. This more direct emotional processing can help her speak more openly about frustration with her own changing body, instead of carrying it silently.

SE2: Practical acts of help for others were a source of meaning to the self-preservation Two for years; when trembling or stiffness make exactly these tasks harder, it strikes not only her mobility but her self-understanding as a giver.
SO2: Slowed movement and growing fatigue can limit the social Two's accustomed availability to many people, which she often initially finds harder to accept than the physical symptoms themselves.
SX2: In her one important relationship, the sexual Two already engaged in mutual give and take. This openness often makes it easier for her to accept support with everyday tasks from exactly this person, rather than resisting it.

SE3: Efficiency and a brisk working pace mattered to the self-preservation Three for years; a disease that inevitably slows movement fundamentally challenges her accustomed functioning and demands a new understanding of productivity from her.
SO3: The social Three carefully cultivated her poised public appearance; a mask-like facial expression or visible tremor in public can therefore particularly unsettle her, because it involuntarily reveals what she never wanted to show.
SX3: The sexual Three already let her flawless facade drop earlier, but only in front of the one person who mattered to her. This already familiar protected space makes it easier for her to be more open about visible symptom …

Epilepsy (Psychosomatik-Register · Nervous System & Psyche)
A neurological disease involving recurrent seizures, in which nerve cells in the brain suddenly discharge in an uncontrolled, synchronized way.
Definition: Epilepsy is a neurological disease characterized by recurrent epileptic seizures – sudden, uncontrolled electrical discharges of groups of nerve cells in the brain that can take very different forms depending on the brain region affected: from brief absence seizures with a pause in consciousness, through focal seizures with isolated motor or sensory symptoms, to generalized tonic-clonic seizures with loss of consciousness and convulsions throughout the body. The causes are varied: genetic predisposition, brain damage from accidents, strokes, infections, or tumors, brain malformations, or – in a considerable proportion of those affected – no clear cause can be found despite thorough diagnostic workup. With appropriate medication, the majority of those affected achieve good seizure control or complete freedom from seizures.
Typische Symptome: Sudden brief lapses in consciousness (absence seizures); Involuntary jerking of individual body parts or the whole body; Temporary speech, vision, or sensory disturbances during a focal seizure; Loss of consciousness with falling and generalized convulsions; Unusual sensations or a warning feeling (aura) before some seizures; Confusion, exhaustion, or sore muscles after a seizure; In some forms, tongue biting or involuntary loss of bladder control during the seizure
Notfall-Hinweis: An epileptic seizure is a medical emergency requiring an immediate call to emergency services if it lasts longer than five minutes, or if several seizures occur in a row without the person fully regaining consciousness in between (status epilepticus), if it is the person's very first seizure ever, if the seizure is accompanied by an injury, a fall from height, occurs in water, or involves breathing difficulties, or if the person does not regain consciousness within a few minutes after the seizure. During a seizure: protect the person from injury, do not put anything in their mouth, if possible move them into the stable recovery position, and time the seizure.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Here too, the most important thing comes first: epilepsy does not arise from a particular personality or a psychological pattern, but from neurological causes – genetic predisposition, brain damage, a malformation, or, in many of those affected, with no findable cause at all. No subtype falls ill more often or bears responsibility for their own seizures. What differs among the 27 subtypes is solely how a person lives with the unpredictability of a seizure that can in principle strike at any time, how they handle the often stigmatized public image of epilepsy, how they involve family and their surroundings, and how they balance safety precautions with the wish for as normal an everyday life as possible. This section describes exactly these different paths of coping – never a cause.
--- Typ 1: When control becomes impossible in the moment of a seizure ---

SO1: Being seen publicly as reliable and composed mattered to the social One throughout her life; the worry of having a seizure precisely in public and losing control there can weigh on her more heavily than the medical risk itself.
SX1: The sexual One discharges her feelings more immediately than other One variants; this more direct expression can help her speak more openly about fear of the next seizure, instead of carrying it silently the way other One variants tend to.

SO2: Being available for others at all times mattered to the social Two; the need to let those close to her know about her condition and how to act in an emergency is often experienced by her not as a burden but as a new way of forging connection.
SX2: The sexual Two already lived mutual care rather than one-sided giving in her one important relationship; making exactly this person her trusted contact for emergencies therefore comes more easily to her than the purely giving role adopted by other Two variants.

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) (Psychosomatik-Register · Nervous System & Psyche)
A rare, rapidly progressing disease of the nervous system in which the nerve cells for voluntary muscle movement increasingly die, while the mind usually stays clear.
Definition: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rare, incurable, and usually rapidly progressing neurodegenerative disease in which the motor nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord responsible for voluntary muscle control gradually die off. The result is progressive muscle weakness and wasting that can eventually affect almost all voluntarily controlled muscles – from the limbs to the muscles used for speech and swallowing to the respiratory muscles – while sensory perception, bladder and bowel function, and, in the large majority of those affected, cognitive function remain intact. In about 90 percent of cases, ALS occurs with no discernible family history; in around 10 percent, an inherited, genetically caused form is present. The precise triggering mechanisms are still not fully understood despite intensive research; an interplay of genetic predisposition, disturbed protein metabolism in nerve cells, and, in a small proportion of cases, possible environmental factors is discussed.
Typische Symptome: Progressive muscle weakness, usually starting in one hand, arm, or leg; Muscle twitching (fasciculations) and increasing muscle wasting; Speech and swallowing difficulties when the muscles of the mouth and throat are involved; Increasing respiratory weakness as the disease progresses; Preserved sensory perception and, for most of those affected, preserved cognitive function; Muscle cramps and increased reflexes; Emotional lability with involuntary laughing or crying in some forms of the disease
Notfall-Hinweis: Call emergency services immediately for sudden severe shortness of breath or risk of choking from swallowing difficulty. Because ALS progressively weakens the respiratory muscles, close attachment to a specialized ALS center is important, so that support such as assisted ventilation, feeding tubes, and an advance directive can be discussed in good time, before an acute crisis occurs.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Here too, the most important thing comes first: ALS does not arise from a particular personality, from strength or weakness of character, or from a psychological pattern, but from the progressive death of motor nerve cells – caused by genetic predisposition, disturbed protein metabolism in nerve cells, and, in a small proportion of cases, possible environmental factors. No subtype carries a higher risk, and no one is responsible for this disease through their own behavior or thinking. What differs among the 27 subtypes is solely how a person lives with the rapid, often especially cruel contrast of a mind that usually stays clear while the body increasingly fails to obey – how they communicate once speaking is no longer possible, how they cope with growing complete dependence on family and care, and what role they must renegotiate in their closest relationships. This section describes these different ways of coping – never a cause, and never a judgment on how someone handles this especially difficult diagnosis.

Liver Cancer (Psychosomatik-Register · Oncology)
A malignant tumor of the liver that usually develops on the basis of an already damaged liver and causes few symptoms for a long time.
Definition: Liver cancer (most commonly hepatocellular carcinoma) is a malignant tumor arising from liver tissue itself – distinct from liver metastases of other cancers. Bladder Cancer (Psychosomatik-Register · Oncology)
A malignant tumor of the bladder lining that usually appears in older age and often first shows itself as painless blood in the urine.
Definition: Bladder cancer (most commonly urothelial carcinoma) is a malignant tumor arising from the lining of the bladder. By far the largest risk factor is smoking, which contributes to a substantial share of all cases. Other recognized causes include longstanding occupational exposure to certain chemicals (for example in the dye, rubber, or textile industries), chronic bladder irritation, and, in some parts of the world, certain parasitic infections. Ovarian Cancer (Psychosomatik-Register · Oncology)
A malignant tumor of the ovaries that for a long time causes vague or no symptoms at all, and is therefore often discovered late.
Definition: Ovarian cancer is a malignant tumor arising from the ovaries or the neighboring fallopian tubes. Recognized risk factors include older age, hereditary predispositions such as mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, a family history of ovarian or breast cancer, never having given birth, and certain forms of endometriosis. Long-term use of the contraceptive pill, by contrast, has been shown to lower the risk. Because the ovaries lie deep within the pelvis and early tumors barely cause symptoms, the usually vague symptoms such as bloating or a feeling of fullness are often misread for a long time, so the disease is frequently only recognized at an advanced stage. Treatment generally consists of surgical removal of the tumor tissue, usually combined with chemotherapy; where a BRCA mutation is confirmed, targeted drugs may also be considered. The prognosis depends crucially on the stage at diagnosis.

Cervical Cancer (Psychosomatik-Register · Oncology)
A malignant tumor of the cervix that in the vast majority of cases develops from infection with certain HPV types and is well detectable through screening.
Definition: Cervical cancer is a malignant tumor arising from the tissue of the cervix. The overwhelming cause is a persistent infection with certain high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV) – an extremely common viral infection that most sexually active people encounter at some point in life, and which in the vast majority of cases clears on its own without ever developing into disease. Only in a small proportion of infections does the virus persist for years, gradually promoting cell changes and eventually cancer. Other contributing factors are smoking, a weakened immune system, and the absence of regular screening. HPV vaccination significantly lowers the risk, and the Pap smear usually detects precursor changes years before they could develop into cancer – which is why cervical cancer is among the cancers best preventable through screening. Treatment ranges from surgical removal of altered tissue to removal of the uterus to radiation and chemotherapy; the prognosis is generally very good when caught early.
Typische Symptome: Unusual vaginal bleeding, for example between periods or after menopause; Bleeding after intercourse; Unusual, foul-smelling discharge; Pain in the pelvis or lower back; Pain during intercourse; Unexplained weight loss at an advanced stage
Notfall-Hinweis: Unusual bleeding, especially after intercourse or after menopause, should be checked by a doctor promptly – regular screening usually detects changes even before such symptoms appear. With known cervical cancer accompanied by heavy bleeding, severe pain, or fever, seek medical help immediately.

Definition: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is not a single disease but a highly diverse group of malignant conditions of the lymphatic system, arising from degenerated white blood cells (lymphocytes) that can spread through lymph nodes, spleen, bone marrow, and sometimes other organs. Type 1 Diabetes (Psychosomatik-Register · Hormones & Metabolism)
An autoimmune condition in which the body's own immune system destroys the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas – usually beginning already in childhood or adolescence, independent of lifestyle or diet.
Definition: Type 1 diabetes mellitus is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas. Unlike type 2, type 1 has nothing to do with excess weight, diet, or lifestyle – its exact triggers are still not fully understood, though a genetic predisposition combined with environmental factors, possibly certain viral infections, is discussed. The condition typically appears already in childhood, adolescence, or young adulthood, often within a few weeks and with pronounced symptoms. Because the body can no longer produce its own insulin, those affected depend on external supply for life – through injections or an insulin pump – and must check their blood sugar several times a day. This illness is never the result of poor choices; it is a chronic underlying condition that demands a high degree of self-management from the very start, often from childhood on.
Typische Symptome: Intense thirst and very frequent urination; Rapid, unexplained weight loss; Pronounced fatigue and weakness; Ravenous hunger despite weight loss; Nausea, abdominal pain, acetone-like breath odor when blood sugar derails; Visual disturbances from fluctuating blood sugar levels
Notfall-Hinweis: Call emergency services immediately for clouded consciousness, acetone-like breath odor, severe nausea, and rapid breathing (suspected diabetic ketoacidosis). Also act immediately for severe hypoglycemia with confusion or unconsciousness.

A fat metabolism thrown out of balance, in which cholesterol or triglycerides accumulate in the blood without those affected usually feeling anything – until the vessels take damage.
Definition: Hyperlipidemia or dyslipidemia describes a disorder of fat metabolism in which blood lipid levels – particularly LDL cholesterol and triglycerides – remain persistently elevated, while protective HDL cholesterol often stays too low. Causes can include a genetic predisposition (familial hypercholesterolemia), diet, lack of exercise, excess weight, but also other underlying conditions such as an underactive thyroid or diabetes. The insidious part: elevated blood lipid levels usually cause no noticeable symptoms for years, while deposits (plaques) quietly form in the vessel walls, considerably raising the risk of atherosclerosis, heart attack, and stroke. The diagnosis is usually made incidentally through a blood test, often only after lipid levels have already been too high, unnoticed, for years.

The course usually unfolds slowly over years, and many men unknowingly adjust to the gradual restriction before recognizing it as something that needs treatment.
