Cataract (Psychosomatik-Register · Eyes)
A usually age-related clouding of the eye's lens, in which the world is increasingly perceived as if through a veil or a fogged-up pane of glass.
Definition: A cataract is a progressive clouding of the eye's lens, which is normally clear and directs light unimpeded onto the retina. By far the most common cause is the natural aging process, in which protein structures in the lens change and cloud over; less commonly, congenital forms, injuries, certain medications (such as cortisone), or accompanying conditions like diabetes are responsible. Unlike glaucoma, where the optic nerve is damaged by elevated pressure, a cataract affects the lens itself – the world does not narrow but grows increasingly milky, blurred, and low in contrast, as if seen through a fogged windowpane. The course usually unfolds slowly over years; surgery with lens replacement is now considered a routine procedure with very good outcomes.
Typische Symptome: Increasingly blurred, hazy vision; Diminishing contrast and color perception; Heightened glare sensitivity, especially in darkness and against bright light; Double vision in one eye; Frequent changes in eyeglass prescription; Reduced vision at dusk and while driving at night
Notfall-Hinweis: A cataract itself is not an acute emergency and usually develops over years. Still, sudden, one-sided vision loss, severe eye pain, or flashes of light with a shower of dark spots should be evaluated promptly by an ophthalmologist to rule out other, acute causes.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
With a cataract, the field of vision does not narrow, as with glaucoma – instead, what is seen loses its clarity, as if a veil were settling over one's own perception with the years. Psychosomatically, this often suggests an image of growing blur in the view of one's own future or past – as though some things, consciously or unconsciously, are no longer meant to be seen quite so sharply. In TCM, dimming, weakening eyesight in old age is often linked to declining liver blood and kidney essence, the foundations that nourish the eye over a long life. Each of the 27 subtypes reveals its own pattern of what stays consciously or unconsciously out of focus here.

Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD) (Psychosomatik-Register · Eyes)
A progressive disease of the point of sharpest vision at the center of the retina, in which the central gaze itself – on faces, letters, whatever is looked at directly – gets lost.
Definition: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) affects the macula, the point of sharpest vision at the center of the retina responsible for direct, detailed sight – such as reading, recognizing faces, or driving. A distinction is made between the more common, more slowly progressing dry form, in which visual cells in the macular region gradually die off, and the rarer but more aggressive wet form, in which abnormal, leaky blood vessels grow beneath the retina and can rapidly lead to vision loss. Unlike a cataract, which clouds the lens, or glaucoma, which narrows the outer edges of the visual field, AMD affects precisely the center of the field of view – peripheral vision usually remains intact for a long time, while a growing gap or distorted spot forms at the center. Risk factors include age, family history, smoking, and certain dietary factors.
Typische Symptome: Blurred or distorted vision at the center of the field of view; Straight lines appear wavy or bent; Increasing difficulty reading and recognizing faces; A gray or dark spot at the center of the visual field; Diminishing color vision and contrast sensitivity; Preserved, usually unremarkable peripheral vision
Notfall-Hinweis: Have sudden, rapid deterioration of central vision or newly appearing distorted lines (a possible sign of the wet form of AMD) evaluated promptly by an ophthalmologist, since early treatment can be decisive for preserving eyesight.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
With macular degeneration, what is lost is precisely what the gaze is directed at – the face of the person opposite, the word on the page, whatever stands right at the center of attention – while the edge of the visual field remains intact. Psychosomatically, this often suggests an image of a center that withdraws from the direct gaze – as though what is closest and most personal becomes increasingly hard to grasp clearly, while everything around it stays visible. Each of the 27 subtypes reveals its own pattern of what becomes harder to hold at one's own center here.

Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD) (Psychosomatik-Register · Cardiovascular System)
When the legs no longer keep up on a path that has long since grown too narrow.
Definition: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD), colloquially known as „intermittent claudication“ or „window-shopper's disease,“ refers to a usually arteriosclerotic narrowing or blockage of the arteries in the legs (less commonly the arms). Under exertion, the muscles no longer receive enough oxygen, causing exertion-dependent pain that typically forces a stop after a short walking distance – hence the nickname: sufferers appear to pause in front of shop windows, but are actually waiting for the pain to subside. Left untreated, PAD can progress to critical ischemia with the threat of tissue loss.
Typische Symptome: Exertion-dependent, cramp-like pain in the calf, thigh, or buttock that forces a stop after a short walking distance and quickly eases at rest; Cool, pale skin on the legs or feet, weakened or absent pulses; Poorly healing wounds or ulcers on toes or feet; In advanced stages: pain at rest, including at night, that improves when the leg is dangled; Hair loss on the lower legs, brittle toenails as signs of reduced blood flow
Notfall-Hinweis: In the case of sudden, severe pain with a pale, cold, numb limb (acute arterial occlusion) or signs of dying tissue (blackening, a spreading wound that shows no sign of healing): call emergency services immediately or go to an emergency room without delay. An acute vascular occlusion is a time-critical emergency in which every hour can decide whether the limb is saved – there is no room for psychosomatic interpretation here.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
PAD strikes people quite literally where they move: in the legs, the tool we use to travel toward or away from something. Conventional medicine sees mainly arteriosclerosis, favored by smoking, diabetes, and high blood pressure. Pulmonary Embolism (Psychosomatik-Register · Cardiovascular System)
When a sudden blockage of the lung takes away breath that was already scarce.
Definition: A pulmonary embolism occurs when a blood clot (thrombus) – usually originating in the deep leg veins – travels through the bloodstream into the pulmonary arteries and blocks one or more vessels there. Depending on the size of the blockage, the clinical picture ranges from barely noticeable symptoms to acute circulatory collapse. Risk factors include prolonged immobility, surgery, pregnancy, smoking, obesity, and inherited clotting disorders.
Typische Symptome: Sudden-onset shortness of breath, often at rest and without an obvious trigger; Sharp, breath-dependent chest pain; Rapid heartbeat, dizziness up to fainting; Coughing, in some cases with blood-streaked sputum; Often accompanied by: swelling, pain, or warmth in one leg as a sign of deep vein thrombosis; A feeling of anxiety and constriction that goes beyond mere breathlessness
Notfall-Hinweis: A pulmonary embolism is ALWAYS an acute medical emergency. In the case of sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain, dizziness, fainting, or coughing blood: call emergency services immediately. This holds regardless of how mild the symptoms seem and regardless of how well the affected person still feels in the moment – a blockage can worsen dramatically within minutes. There is no room for psychosomatic interpretation here, only for immediate emergency care.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Few conditions in this compass show as vividly how something accumulated unnoticed for a long time can suddenly break loose and take the breath away: a clot that formed quietly and mostly unnoticed in a leg vein travels through the bloodstream to the lungs and, within seconds, blocks exactly what the body otherwise needs to breathe freely. Psychosomatics often reads in this an image of something held back for a long time that suddenly releases and strikes exactly where life is felt most immediately – in the breath.

Aortic Aneurysm (Psychosomatik-Register · Cardiovascular System)
When the body's largest artery gives way under years of pressure, quietly and without warning.
Definition: An aortic aneurysm is a pathological, usually arteriosclerotic bulging of the main artery (aorta), most often in the abdomen (abdominal aortic aneurysm), less commonly in the chest (thoracic aneurysm). High blood pressure, smoking, genetic predisposition, or inflammatory processes cause the vessel wall to lose elasticity and slowly expand over years. As long as the aneurysm does not rupture, it usually causes no symptoms at all and is often discovered by chance during an examination.
Typische Symptome: Usually no symptoms for years – the aneurysm grows silently; With larger aneurysms, occasional diffuse back or abdominal pain, a pulsating sensation in the abdomen; When pressing on surrounding structures: a feeling of fullness, difficulty swallowing (with thoracic aneurysm), hoarseness; Sudden, extremely severe, devastating pain in the abdomen, back, or chest as a sign of an impending or actual rupture; In the event of rupture: circulatory collapse, paleness, loss of consciousness
Notfall-Hinweis: A ruptured aneurysm is an acutely life-threatening emergency. In the case of sudden, extremely severe abdominal, back, or chest pain, especially combined with circulatory collapse, paleness, or clouded consciousness: call emergency services immediately. An untreated ruptured aortic aneurysm leads to death within a very short time – every minute counts, and there is no room here for psychosomatic interpretation, only for immediate emergency care.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.

An aneurysm forms where this wall can no longer withstand that pressure over the years and slowly, silently expands – until it gives way, often without any warning. Psychosomatics often reads in this the image of a baseline tension carried for years, barely visible from the outside, yet stretching one's own substance from within until the limit of what can be borne is eventually reached.

Cardiomyopathy (Psychosomatik-Register · Cardiovascular System)
When the heart muscle itself loses its shape, independent of the vessels that supply it.
Definition: Cardiomyopathies are diseases of the heart muscle itself that are not primarily caused by narrowed coronary arteries or high blood pressure. Distinctions include dilated cardiomyopathy (the heart muscle weakens and the chambers widen, pumping power declines), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (the heart muscle thickens pathologically, often genetically caused), and so-called stress cardiomyopathy („broken heart syndrome,“ Takotsubo syndrome), which typically occurs acutely after extreme emotional or physical strain and shows the link between emotional shock and heart function especially directly.
Typische Symptome: Increasing shortness of breath, initially under exertion, later also at rest; Rapid exhaustion, reduced physical capacity; Heart rhythm disturbances, palpitations, racing heart; Fluid retention (edema) in the legs or abdomen as a sign of heart failure; In stress cardiomyopathy: sudden, heart-attack-like chest pain immediately after severe emotional shock, without an actual vascular blockage; Dizziness, in severe cases fainting
Notfall-Hinweis: In the case of sudden chest pain, acute shortness of breath, fainting, or suspected acute heart failure (e.g. after severe emotional strain): call emergency services immediately, since it is clinically nearly impossible to distinguish a true vascular blockage from an acute cardiomyopathy. With a known cardiomyopathy and sudden deterioration (severe shortness of breath, marked weight gain from fluid retention, clouded consciousness): also seek emergency medical care without delay.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Stress cardiomyopathy, aptly nicknamed „broken heart syndrome,“ is one of the few cardiac diagnoses in which the link between emotional shock and heart function is medically recognized directly: after the death of a loved one, a breakup, or a shock event, the left heart chamber can acutely deform in a way that resembles, on imaging, a traditional Japanese octopus trap (takotsubo). The other cardiomyopathies, too, affect the heart muscle itself, not merely its blood supply – psychosomatics often reads in this the question of how much emotional shock, sustained strain, or suppressed grief a heart muscle can carry over time before its very shape begins to change.

That of all things the heart muscle itself changes pathologically, even while everything outwardly stays disciplined, can be read as the bodily irony of a life that controlled almost everything except its own heartbeat.

Gastritis (Psychosomatik-Register · Digestive System)
When the stomach lining reacts, inflamed, to what the stomach can no longer digest.
Definition: Gastritis is an inflammation of the stomach lining that can be acute (often caused by alcohol, medications such as pain relievers, stress, or an infection) or chronic. The most common cause of chronic gastritis is infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori; autoimmune processes or chronic irritation from bile reflux play a role less often. Left untreated, chronic gastritis can raise the risk of stomach ulcers and, in rare cases, stomach cancer.
Typische Symptome: A feeling of pressure or fullness in the upper abdomen, often after eating; Nausea, occasional vomiting; Burning or gnawing pain in the upper abdomen; Loss of appetite, feeling full prematurely; Belching, heartburn; In acute gastritis with a tendency to bleed: vomiting blood or black-colored stool (warning sign)
Notfall-Hinweis: In the case of vomiting blood, black, tarry stool, sudden severe abdominal pain, or circulatory weakness: seek emergency medical care immediately or call emergency services, as this can indicate acute stomach bleeding. There is no room for psychosomatic interpretation here, only for immediate medical evaluation.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.

Pulmonary Fibrosis (Psychosomatik-Register · Respiratory System & Lungs)
When lung tissue scars over the years and the space to breathe slowly narrows.
Definition: Pulmonary fibrosis refers to a progressive, usually irreversible scarring (fibrosis) of lung tissue, which makes the lungs increasingly stiff and impairs gas exchange. In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, the most common form, the exact cause remains unknown; but it can also be triggered by autoimmune diseases, long-term exposure to dust or mold, certain medications, or chronic reflux. The disease usually progresses gradually over years, with steadily declining lung function.
Typische Symptome: Increasing shortness of breath, initially under exertion, over time also at rest; Dry, persistent irritant cough without sputum; Rapid exhaustion, declining physical capacity; Unintended weight loss in advanced stages; Clubbed fingers (club-shaped thickening of the fingertips) as a late sign of chronic oxygen deficiency; Bluish discoloration of the lips or fingertips in advanced disease
Notfall-Hinweis: In the case of suddenly worsening, severe shortness of breath, bluish discoloration of the lips or fingertips, or an acute deterioration in known pulmonary fibrosis: seek emergency medical care immediately or call emergency services, as this can indicate an acute exacerbation. There is no room for psychosomatic interpretation here, only for immediate medical evaluation.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
The lungs are the organ through which we exchange with the world most directly – every breath a taking in and a letting go. When the tissue scars, exactly this exchange becomes increasingly restricted: the lungs grow stiffer, the space for air narrower, without the process being reversible. Traditional Chinese Medicine traditionally links the lungs with grief and letting go. Psychosomatics often reads in the progressing scarring an image of a living space narrowed over years, of grief that could never fully release, or of an exchange with the world that has grown increasingly rigid.

Hepatitis B (Chronic) (Psychosomatik-Register · Immune System & Autoimmune)
A liver inflammation that doesn't heal but becomes a permanent companion – raising the question of who to tell and who not to.
Definition: Chronic hepatitis B is an inflammation of the liver, persisting for at least six months, caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), which can be transmitted through blood, sexual contact, or from mother to child. In a small proportion of those infected – especially when infection occurs in adulthood – the infection does not fully resolve, and the virus remains permanently detectable in the liver. Left untreated, chronic hepatitis B can lead over years to liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, or, in rare cases, liver cancer. Modern antiviral medications, however, can reliably suppress viral replication in most affected people and keep the disease course stable for decades – chronic hepatitis B is thus, for the great majority of those affected, a well-manageable long-term condition today, not an automatic precursor to liver failure. How an infection was acquired says nothing about the character of the person affected.
Typische Symptome: Often no or only nonspecific symptoms for years (fatigue, mild discomfort in the upper right abdomen); Occasional yellowing of skin and eyes during acute flares; Elevated liver enzymes as a common incidental finding on routine tests; In late stages, signs of liver cirrhosis (fluid retention, bleeding tendency); Psychological strain from the diagnosis, disclosure questions, and uncertainty about the future
Notfall-Hinweis: See a doctor immediately for severe jaundice, confusion, bleeding, or severe abdominal pain – these can indicate acute liver decompensation.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
How a chronic hepatitis B infection was acquired plays no role in this psychosomatic reflection and carries no moral judgment whatsoever – what matters here is exclusively how a person handles the diagnosis itself: the decision of who to tell and who not to, the question of treatment adherence over the years, and the navigation of closeness and intimacy once a permanent infection has become part of one's own life. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct pattern emerges in how they handle disclosure, treatment discipline, and their own vulnerability toward others.

Hepatitis C (Chronic) (Psychosomatik-Register · Immune System & Autoimmune)
A liver infection that is usually curable today – but the path to diagnosis is often a long one of not knowing.
Definition: Chronic hepatitis C is an inflammation of the liver, persisting for at least six months, caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV), which is transmitted mainly through blood contact – for instance through shared needles, contaminated medical instruments in the past, or, more rarely, sexual contact. Left untreated, chronic hepatitis C can lead to liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, or liver cancer. Since the introduction of modern direct-acting antiviral medications, hepatitis C can be completely cured within a few weeks in the vast majority of those affected – a decisive medical advance over the considerably more arduous therapies of the past. How an infection was acquired says nothing about the character of the person affected.

HIV / AIDS (Psychosomatik-Register · Immune System & Autoimmune)
A diagnosis that today, with modern treatment, allows for a normal, long life – and yet remains bound up with deep-seated social stigma to this day.
Definition: HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) is a virus that specifically attacks certain cells of the immune system and, left untreated, can lead over years to their progressive weakening, until the stage of AIDS is reached, in which the body can no longer build adequate defenses even against normally harmless pathogens. Transmission occurs through certain bodily fluids, most commonly through unprotected sexual contact or shared needles. Since the 1990s, treatment has been fundamentally transformed by antiretroviral therapy (ART): with regular use of modern medications, the amount of virus in the blood can be reduced to the point of being undetectable – those affected thereby achieve a nearly normal life expectancy and can no longer transmit the virus sexually (›Undetectable = Untransmittable‹). HIV is thus, for people with access to treatment, a well-manageable chronic condition today, not a death sentence. How an infection was acquired says nothing about the character of the person affected, and the social stigma still widely attached to those affected bears no relation to the actual medical risk under treatment.
Typische Symptome: Often flu-like symptoms shortly after infection, which are easily overlooked; Frequently no or only nonspecific symptoms for years without treatment; In the advanced, untreated stage, recurring infections due to weakened immune defenses; Under effective therapy, usually no disease-related symptoms; Considerable psychological strain from the shock of diagnosis, stigma experience, and disclosure decisions
Notfall-Hinweis: See a doctor promptly if an acute HIV infection is suspected, or with a known infection and a sudden cluster of unusually severe infectious illnesses.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.

The social stigma that continues to accompany HIV to this day is itself an independent psychological burden, separate from the medical course of the disease. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct pattern emerges in how they handle disclosure, treatment discipline, and their own vulnerability toward others.

Tuberculosis (Psychosomatik-Register · Immune System & Autoimmune)
A bacterial infection that mainly affects the lungs and demands weeks to months of isolation and treatment adherence.
Definition: Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which primarily affects the lungs but can in principle involve other organs as well. Transmission occurs through airborne droplets when coughing, usually with close and prolonged contact. Not every infection leads to active disease – in many people, the bacterium remains in an inactive, latent form in the body for years without causing symptoms. When the disease does become active, it is generally curable with a several-months combination therapy of multiple antibiotics, though this requires a high degree of treatment adherence throughout, since an interrupted course of therapy can lead to resistance. During the contagious phase, temporary isolation is also necessary to prevent further spread.
Typische Symptome: Persistent cough lasting more than three weeks, sometimes with traces of blood; Night sweats and gradual weight loss; Ongoing fatigue and loss of appetite; Mild fever over an extended period; Chest pain when breathing or coughing
Notfall-Hinweis: See a doctor immediately for severe coughing up of blood or severe shortness of breath.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Tuberculosis confronts those affected with an unusual double demand: months of uninterrupted treatment adherence, and, during the contagious phase, an enforced isolation from precisely the people who would otherwise provide support. In TCM, such a state is often interpreted as a deep-seated weakness of Lung Yin, associated with inner restlessness and a gradual loss of vitality. Psychosomatically, tuberculosis often reads as an image of forced slowing down and separation that fundamentally contradicts one's own life rhythm. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct pattern emerges in how they handle the long duration of treatment and the temporary isolation.

Lyme Disease (from Tick Bites) (Psychosomatik-Register · Immune System & Autoimmune)
A bacterial infection following a tick bite, usually well treatable when caught early, but able to progress insidiously if left untreated.
Definition: Lyme disease is an infectious disease caused by bacteria of the genus Borrelia, transmitted through the bite of an infected tick. A typical, though not universal, early sign is erythema migrans, a ring-shaped skin rash spreading outward from the bite site. Left untreated, the infection can spread after weeks to months to the joints, the nervous system, or the heart, causing varied and sometimes hard-to-place symptoms there. When caught early, Lyme disease is generally well treatable with a course of antibiotics usually lasting two to four weeks. Because symptoms can vary so widely and a tick bite often goes unnoticed, diagnosis is sometimes made only after a prolonged phase of nonspecific complaints.
Typische Symptome: Erythema migrans around the bite site in the first days to weeks (not present in everyone affected); Flu-like symptoms such as fatigue, headache, and body aches; In later stages, joint pain and swelling, especially in large joints; Nerve pain, paralysis symptoms, or sensory disturbances with neurological involvement; Heart rhythm disturbances with rare cardiac involvement
Notfall-Hinweis: See a doctor promptly for acute paralysis symptoms, severe nerve pain, or heart rhythm disturbances.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Lyme disease often strikes people unexpectedly out of an entirely ordinary everyday situation – a walk, gardening, an outing in nature – without any basis for implying carelessness. Precisely because the bite itself often goes unnoticed and symptoms can develop gradually and ambiguously, the illness confronts those affected with the particular challenge of facing a diffuse, hard-to-grasp set of complaints. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct pattern emerges in how they handle this ambiguity between early suspicion, delayed diagnosis, and treatment.

Anorexia Nervosa (Psychosomatik-Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
An eating disorder in which control over one's own body becomes the central source of stability, while the danger to life and health is pushed aside.
Definition: Anorexia nervosa is a serious eating disorder in which those affected restrict their eating so severely that a markedly low body weight results for their age, height, and build – accompanied by a pronounced fear of weight gain and a distorted perception of one's own body. Self-worth is closely tied to weight and body shape in this illness. Anorexia nervosa is considered one of the mental illnesses with the highest health risks, because it affects the entire organism – the cardiovascular system, hormone balance, bone density. Neurobiologically, genetic predisposition, personality factors such as perfectionism, family and social influences, and often a triggering life event all play a role together. Early, specialized treatment significantly improves the prognosis.
Typische Symptome: Significant weight loss through restricted eating; Pronounced fear of weight gain despite being underweight; Distorted perception of one's own body; Intense preoccupation with food, weight, and body image; Withdrawal from social situations, especially around shared meals; Physical exhaustion and difficulty concentrating; Absence of menstruation in affected women
Notfall-Hinweis: In cases of severe underweight, circulatory problems, cardiac arrhythmia, or other physical warning signs, immediate medical evaluation is necessary – anorexia nervosa can have life-threatening physical consequences. Likewise, in the case of suicidal thoughts, contact a crisis hotline immediately or call emergency services. Specialized eating-disorder treatment should be sought early, not only once things reach an acute crisis.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
In anorexia nervosa, one's own body becomes the last place where control still seems possible, while much else feels uncontrollable all around. Psychosomatically, this illness often reads as the picture of an inner battle for stability, worth, and self-determination that – for reasons that differ from subtype to subtype – discharges specifically around food. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct emotional pattern can underlie this struggle.

Bulimia Nervosa (Psychosomatik-Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
An eating disorder in which loss of control and attempts at control alternate in a recurring cycle, usually hidden from view.
Definition: Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by recurring episodes of losing control while eating, followed by behaviors intended to undo the feared weight gain. Unlike anorexia nervosa, body weight in bulimia nervosa is often within the normal range, which frequently keeps the illness invisible from the outside for a long time. Those affected usually experience the episodes as shameful and try to keep them strictly secret. Here too, self-worth is closely tied to weight and body shape. Neurobiologically and psychologically, a combination of genetic predisposition, perfectionism, difficulty with emotional regulation, and social pressure toward thinness play a role together. Left untreated, bulimia nervosa can have significant physical consequences, particularly for electrolyte balance and the cardiovascular system.
Typische Symptome: Recurring episodes of losing control while eating; Subsequent compensatory behaviors, often carried out in secret; Intense feelings of shame and guilt surrounding these episodes; Strong dependence of self-worth on weight and body shape; Frequently an inconspicuous, normal-weight outward appearance; Physical exhaustion, throat discomfort, dental damage; Social withdrawal around shared meals
Notfall-Hinweis: In the presence of physical warning signs such as cardiac arrhythmia, severe exhaustion, or circulatory problems, immediate medical evaluation is necessary – a disturbed electrolyte balance can become life-threatening. In the case of suicidal thoughts, contact a crisis hotline immediately or call emergency services. Specialized eating-disorder treatment should be sought early, not only once things reach an acute crisis.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Bulimia nervosa often lives a kind of double life – unremarkable on the outside, while on the inside it is shaped by a recurring alternation between losing control and desperately trying to regain it, something almost no one nearby ever notices. Psychosomatically, this illness often reads as the picture of an inner pressure that can no longer be contained, followed by an equally strong fear of the consequences of that loss of control. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct emotional pattern can underlie this swing between outbreak and retreat.

Binge Eating Disorder (Psychosomatik-Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
An eating disorder in which recurring loss of control while eating, without any compensatory behavior afterward, leads to deep shame and often social withdrawal.
Definition: Binge eating disorder is characterized by recurring episodes of losing control while eating, in which a person eats substantially more in a short time than they themselves consider appropriate – without the compensatory behaviors typical of bulimia nervosa. The episodes are usually experienced as highly distressing, accompanied by strong feelings of shame and guilt, often eaten in secret and without any physical sensation of hunger. Unlike the occasional overeating that happens on special occasions, this is a recurring pattern with a clear degree of suffering. Neurobiologically and psychologically, a combination of difficulty with emotional regulation, genetic predisposition, and often a history of dieting or restrictive eating play a role. Specialized treatment can effectively break the cycle of loss of control and shame.
Typische Symptome: Recurring episodes of pronounced loss of control while eating; Eating noticeably faster than usual, often without genuine hunger; Eating until uncomfortably full; Intense feelings of shame and guilt after the episodes; Eating in secret out of embarrassment about the amount; No regular use of compensatory behaviors; Frequently accompanying depressive mood or anxiety
Notfall-Hinweis: In the case of severe depressive mood or suicidal thoughts, contact a crisis hotline immediately or call emergency services. If accompanying physical complaints such as severe exhaustion or circulatory problems occur, these should be medically evaluated. Specialized eating-disorder treatment should be sought early, not only once the level of suffering has already become severe.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
In binge eating disorder, the visible counter-movement that often marks bulimia nervosa is absent – what remains is the recurring loss of control itself and the deep shame that follows, often carried in silence for years. Psychosomatically, this illness often reads as the picture of an inner emptiness or pressure that finds no other outlet and therefore seeks a way out through food. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct emotional pattern can underlie this recurring loss of control.

SX1: Directing pressure solely against herself isn't the sexual One's style – she channels it outward instead, which tends to offer her somewhat more protection from the inward-directed pattern of other One variants – though the pattern cannot be entirely ruled out.

Alcohol Use Disorder (Psychosomatik-Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
A recognized, treatable addictive illness in which alcohol increasingly becomes the only reliable way to regulate inner states.
Definition: Alcohol use disorder is a recognized psychological and physical illness, not a question of character weakness or lack of discipline. It is marked by a strong, often difficult-to-control craving for alcohol, an increasing loss of control over the amount and frequency of consumption, tolerance development, and physical withdrawal symptoms upon stopping. Consumption continues despite clearly recognizable negative consequences for health, relationships, and daily life. Neurobiologically, chronic alcohol use lastingly alters the brain's reward system, which turns the illness from a conscious decision into a distinct medical condition. The dependency often functions as a form of self-medication – an attempt to cope with fear, tension, loneliness, or emotional pain. Successful treatment addresses both the physical and psychological dimensions of the illness.
Typische Symptome: Strong, difficult-to-control craving for alcohol; Loss of control over the amount and frequency of consumption; Tolerance development requiring increasing amounts; Physical withdrawal symptoms upon stopping; Continued consumption despite clearly recognizable negative consequences; Neglect of previous interests and social contacts; Increasing preoccupation with obtaining and consuming alcohol
Notfall-Hinweis: Suddenly stopping alcohol on one's own after a long period of severe dependency can be medically dangerous – withdrawal symptoms such as severe tremors, confusion, seizures, or circulatory problems require medical supervision, in a hospital setting if in doubt. Withdrawal should therefore, where possible, take place under medical guidance rather than alone. In the case of suicidal thoughts, contact a crisis hotline immediately or call emergency services. Addiction counseling services offer a low-threshold, confidential first point of contact.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Alcohol use disorder rarely begins as a conscious decision – it usually creeps in over years as a seemingly reliable means of coping with tension, loneliness, or pain, until reaching for the glass becomes a distinct illness beyond one's own control. Psychosomatically, this illness often reads as the picture of an emotional regulation system that came to depend on a chemical shortcut because another path stayed inaccessible for a long time. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct emotional pattern shows what inner tension is meant to be numbed here – and a distinct possible way back.

Medication and Drug Dependence (Psychosomatik-Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
A recognized addictive illness in which prescription medications or illegal substances become the only reliable way to regulate inner states.
Definition: Medication and drug dependence is a recognized psychological and physical illness, not a question of character weakness. It affects both prescription substances such as painkillers, sleep aids, and sedatives, as well as illegal drugs. It is marked by a strong craving for the substance, an increasing loss of control over the amount and frequency of use, tolerance development, and physical and psychological withdrawal symptoms upon stopping. Use continues despite clearly recognizable negative consequences for health, relationships, and daily life. The dependency often develops gradually, sometimes starting from a medically legitimate prescription, or as an attempt to cope with fear, pain, exhaustion, or emotional overload. Neurobiologically, chronic use lastingly alters the brain's reward system. Successful treatment addresses both the physical and psychological dimensions of the illness.
Typische Symptome: Strong, difficult-to-control craving for the substance; Loss of control over the amount and frequency of use; Tolerance development requiring increasing doses; Physical and psychological withdrawal symptoms upon stopping; Continued use despite clearly recognizable negative consequences; Obtaining the substance from multiple doctors or unclear sources; Withdrawal from previous interests and social contacts
Notfall-Hinweis: Suddenly stopping on one's own after prolonged use, particularly of sedatives or painkillers, can be medically dangerous and should take place under medical guidance. In the case of signs of overdose (severe clouding of consciousness, respiratory depression), call emergency services immediately. In the case of suicidal thoughts, contact a crisis hotline immediately. Addiction counseling services offer a low-threshold, confidential first point of contact, even when the substance was originally medically prescribed.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Medication and drug dependence often begins not with a wish for intoxication, but with the understandable need to finally silence pain, fear, or exhaustion – until the substance itself becomes a distinct illness that escapes its original purpose. Psychosomatically, this illness often reads as the picture of an emotional regulation system that came to depend on a chemical shortcut because another path stayed inaccessible for a long time. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct emotional pattern shows what inner state is meant to be numbed or regulated here – and a distinct possible way back.

Social Phobia (Social Anxiety Disorder) (Psychosomatik-Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
A pronounced fear of being judged by others that turns social situations into a constant examination room.
Definition: Social phobia (social anxiety disorder) is marked by a pronounced, persistent fear of social situations in which the person might be exposed to scrutiny by others – conversations, presentations, eating in company, or simply being observed. The main fear is usually acting in an embarrassing or humiliating way, or visibly showing anxiety symptoms such as blushing, trembling, or sweating. These situations are either endured with intense discomfort or consistently avoided, which can significantly limit education, career, and relationships. Neurobiologically, heightened amygdala reactivity to social cues plays a role, favored by genetic predisposition, an anxious temperament in childhood, and humiliating social experiences.
Typische Symptome: Pronounced fear of being judged and watched by others; Avoidance of social situations, or enduring them under great distress; Blushing, trembling, sweating, racing heart in social situations; Constant worry about behaving in an embarrassing way; Excessive self-monitoring during social contact; Avoidance of eye contact; Withdrawal from education, career, or social life
Notfall-Hinweis: In the event of acute suicidal thoughts or complete social isolation accompanied by despair, contact a crisis line immediately (in the US: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, call or text 988) or call emergency services.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Someone living with social phobia enters every room containing other people as if stepping onto a stage with invisible judges seated in the audience – the inward gaze grows so loud that little room remains for genuine contact. In TCM, a state like this is often linked to a weakness of Kidney Water, which normally lends the Heart a sense of security – without it, every encounter becomes a potential danger. Psychosomatically, social phobia often reads as the image of an inner observer who scrutinizes the self more harshly than any onlooker ever would. Each of the 27 subtypes shows its own pattern in what this self-scrutiny fixes on.

Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) (Psychosomatik-Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
A nervous system that fails to register a survived event as over, letting it live on in memories, alarm, and avoidance.
Definition: Post-traumatic stress disorder develops in response to one or more extremely distressing events – such as violence, accidents, war, sexual abuse, or natural disasters – that directly threatened one's own life or someone else's. It is marked by the involuntary reliving of the trauma through flashbacks or nightmares, pronounced avoidance of reminders, persistently heightened tension and a strong startle response, and negative changes in thinking and mood, such as guilt, emotional numbness, or an altered worldview. Symptoms usually appear within the first months after the event and, without treatment, can persist for years. Neurobiologically, a dysregulated stress axis and altered memory processing in the brain are often found, causing the trauma to be experienced not as concluded but as ongoingly present.
Typische Symptome: Involuntary reliving of the trauma (flashbacks, nightmares); Pronounced avoidance of trauma reminders; Persistent hyperarousal and an exaggerated startle response; Concentration and sleep disturbances; Emotional numbness or a sense of detachment; Negative thoughts about oneself or the world; Irritability or outbursts of anger
Notfall-Hinweis: In the event of acute suicidal thoughts, flashbacks with risk of harm to self or others, or dissociative states with loss of control, contact a crisis line immediately (in the US: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, call or text 988) or call emergency services.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
A trauma does not end with the event itself; it goes on living in the nervous system for as long as it hasn't truly been processed – the body keeps standing guard against a danger that is long past. In TCM, a state like this is often associated with startled Kidney Qi, which withdraws from the Heart the grounding it needs after a shock. Psychosomatically, PTSD often reads as the image of an experience too overwhelming to be integrated into one's own life story, so it keeps returning as a constant present. Each of the 27 subtypes shows its own pattern in how it deals with this unresolved experience – though it must be stressed: no subtype makes a trauma more likely, anyone can be affected by one; only the way of processing it afterward differs.

SE1: After a traumatic event, the self-preservation One often searches compulsively for what should have been done differently. This endless self-examination can burden trauma processing further instead of easing it.

SX1: The sexual One directs her anger about what happened outward, at those responsible, rather than primarily turning it against herself. This expression differs from the more inward-directed processing of the other One variants.

SO3: Appearing composed in public remains important to the social Three even after a trauma, which can conceal the true extent of the distress. This facade often makes it harder to seek help in time.
SX3: The sexual Three shows her wound more openly, but only to the one important person, rather than hiding it behind constant capability. This openness sets her apart from the other Three variants' public facade.

Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) (Psychosomatik-Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
Intrusive, tormenting thoughts and actions that can't be willfully stopped, even though the person recognizes their senselessness.
Definition: Obsessive-compulsive disorder is a serious mental illness marked by recurring obsessions – intrusive, distressing thoughts, images, or urges – and/or compulsions, meaning repetitive behaviors or mental rituals performed to reduce the anxiety triggered by the obsessions. Those affected usually recognize their compulsions as excessive or senseless, yet can barely suppress the inner urge to carry them out despite considerable suffering. Common forms include checking, washing, and ordering compulsions, as well as obsessions about contamination, symmetry, or feared misconduct. The disorder is not a character trait and not simply a preference for order, but a clinically distinct condition with substantial time cost and functional impairment. Neurobiologically, changes in cortico-striato-thalamic brain circuits play a role, favored by genetic predisposition and, in some cases, distressing life events.
Typische Symptome: Recurring, intrusive, and distressing obsessions; Repeated compulsions or mental rituals aimed at reducing anxiety; Substantial time spent on compulsions (often over an hour daily); Recognizing the compulsions as senseless while being unable to stop them; Avoidance of situations that trigger obsessions; Strong inner tension when a compulsion is suppressed; Impairment of daily life, work, and relationships
Notfall-Hinweis: In the event of acute suicidal thoughts or obsessions accompanied by urges to harm oneself or others, contact a crisis line immediately (in the US: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, call or text 988) or call emergency services.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner. OCD is not a character trait but a serious, often very distressing clinical condition.
OCD is not an exaggerated sense of order and not an endearing quirk, but a cycle of thought and action that escapes one's own control, no matter how much the person affected wishes otherwise. In TCM, a repeating inner cycle like this is often associated with stagnant Liver Qi paired with a restless Shen, the spirit – a blockage that finds no way out except repetition itself. Psychosomatically, OCD often reads as the image of a deep-seated fear that can be temporarily contained through one specific, repeatable action, without the underlying fear actually being resolved. Each of the 27 subtypes shows its own pattern in what this cycle revolves around.

SX1: The sexual One usually channels her anger over injustice straight outward rather than into inner control rituals. This externalization sets her apart from the more ritualized pattern of the other One variants.

SX3: The sexual Three doesn't have to force a flawless image in front of the one important person, rather than falling into constant control rituals. This relief sets her apart from the public perfectionism of the other Three variants.

Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD in Adults) (Psychosomatik-Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
A neurologically based difference in attention and impulse regulation that often carries daily life through waves of hyperfocus and scatteredness.
Definition: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder, not a character trait, and not a matter of willpower or upbringing. It is based on altered regulation of neurotransmitters such as dopamine and norepinephrine in brain networks responsible for attention control, impulse control, and action planning, and is substantially genetic. In adults, ADHD often presents less as obvious physical hyperactivity and more as inner restlessness, difficulty sustaining or prioritizing attention over longer periods, impulsivity in decisions and conversations, and a pronounced gap between actual potential and what actually gets done day to day. Many people affected develop considerable compensation strategies over the years, which is why the diagnosis in adulthood is frequently missed or only made after decades.
Typische Symptome: Persistent difficulty sustaining attention over longer periods; Pronounced distractibility from external or internal stimuli; Difficulty with organization, prioritization, and time management; Inner restlessness, often without visible motor hyperactivity; Impulsive decisions or statements; Episodes of hyperfocus on especially interesting tasks; Emotional irritability and quick frustration
Notfall-Hinweis: In the event of acute suicidal thoughts, significant self-endangerment through impulsive actions, or complete overwhelm, contact a crisis line immediately (in the US: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, call or text 988) or call emergency services.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner. ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder, not a matter of character or willpower.
ADHD is not a question of type and not a personality style, but a neurologically grounded difference in attention and impulse regulation that occurs regardless of subtype – having it isn't 'explained' by the Enneagram either, only the way it's handled in adult life becomes visibly different from subtype to subtype. Psychosomatically, then, this section isn't about a cause but about coping: how a given subtype handles the everyday consequences of scatteredness, impulsivity, and the often distressing sense of not being able to reliably access one's own potential. Each of the 27 subtypes shows its own pattern in handling this challenge.

SO1: The social One experiences forgotten appointments or unfinished tasks as a moral failing rather than as a symptom. This misreading can significantly deepen shame and self-condemnation.
SX1: The sexual One voices her frustration over her own unreliability directly and immediately, rather than sealing it inside for long. This direct approach sets her apart from the more inward-turned resentment of the other One variants.

SO2: Staying indispensable to many people becomes extra hard for the social Two with ADHD when appointments or commitments get scrambled by her own scatteredness. That can trigger guilt toward many people at once.
SX2: The sexual Two bundles her attention onto the one important person, which with ADHD helps her keep at least this one relationship reliably intact. This focus is a relief compared to the scattering the other Two variants experience.

SO3: Maintaining a flawless public image despite inner disorganization costs the social Three with ADHD a particularly large amount of energy. If this facade does crack, the shame can be intense.
SX3: Masking her scatteredness the way she does in public simply isn't necessary for the sexual Three around the one important person. This relief sets her apart from the public compensation pressure of the other Three variants.

Schizophrenia (Psychosomatik-Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
A severe psychiatric illness involving altered perception of reality, with a strong genetic and neurobiological basis.
Definition: Schizophrenia is a severe psychiatric illness with a pronounced genetic and neurobiological basis, marked by episodic or chronic positive symptoms such as delusions and hallucinations (usually auditory), negative symptoms such as reduced motivation, social withdrawal, and blunted affect, and cognitive impairments affecting concentration and memory, among others. Importantly, schizophrenia is not a 'split personality' and has nothing to do with dissociative identity disorder – this widespread misconception contributes significantly to the stigmatization of those affected. The illness arises from a complex interplay of genetic predisposition, altered brain development and chemistry (particularly in the dopamine system), and environmental factors; it occurs across all cultures and social groups at similar rates. With appropriate medication and psychosocial treatment, many people affected can achieve considerable stabilization and lead self-determined lives.
Typische Symptome: Delusions (e.g. persecutory or referential delusions); Hallucinations, usually auditory (hearing voices); Disorganized thinking and speech; Blunted affect and social withdrawal; Reduced motivation; Cognitive impairments (concentration, memory); Impaired daily functioning during acute phases
Notfall-Hinweis: In the event of an acute psychotic crisis with risk of harm to self or others, acute suicidal thoughts, or a complete break from reality, call emergency services immediately or contact the nearest psychiatric emergency service.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner. Schizophrenia is a severe neurobiological illness; personality or subtype has no causal influence whatsoever on who develops it.
To state this unmistakably up front: schizophrenia is not caused or made more likely by personality, character weakness, or any particular subtype – it has a strong genetic and neurobiological basis, and neither the Enneagram nor any personality model can predict who will develop it. No subtype carries a special vulnerability here, and none is especially protected. What this section describes is therefore explicitly not the origin of the illness itself, but something else: how different people – depending on their basic relational and coping pattern – handle an already-established diagnosis, medication, stigma, and their relationships. Each of the 27 subtypes shows its own pattern here in coping with the illness, never in causing it.
--- Typ 1: A way of handling diagnosis and treatment ---
SE1: Sticking to an exact medication schedule and fixed routines can help the self-preservation One reclaim a piece of control within her treatment. If the diagnosis is experienced as her own failure, though, that can undermine treatment adherence.
SO1: Shame over the social stigma of the illness can weigh especially heavily on the social One, when moral integrity and outward reputation are central to her self-image. Being open with those around her can significantly lighten this burden.
SX1: The sexual One addresses injustices in how others handle her diagnosis directly, rather than silently accepting stigma. This direct approach can help build a supportive environment.
--- Typ 2: A way of handling relationships and disclosure ---
SE2: Worry about becoming a burden to others through her own illness can keep the self-preservation Two from accepting necessary support at all. Actively naming this worry can make it easier to access help.
SO2: Speaking openly about the diagnosis in front of many people is hard for the social Two when stigma heightens her fear of rejection by the wider community. A reliable, closer circle can offer real relief here.
SX2: The sexual Two tends to confide her diagnosis in the one important person rather than in many at once. This one solid relationship can serve as a central anchor of stability in treatment.
--- Typ 3: A way of handling one's own image ---
SE3: Wanting to appear functional despite the illness can lead the self-preservation Three to conceal symptoms or avoid treatment, out of fear of a visible drop in performance. Openness with the treatment team is especially important here.
SO3: The fear of being seen publicly as 'less capable' because of the diagnosis can lead to strong internalized stigma in the social Three. Exchange with other people affected can significantly reduce this burden.
SX3: A flawless image isn't something the sexual Three has to force with the one important person, so she can speak more openly about the illness there. This openness can ease how she copes with the diagnosis.

Bipolar Disorder (Psychosomatik-Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
A severe affective illness with pronounced mood episodes swinging between mania and depression, with a strong genetic basis.
Definition: Bipolar disorder is a severe psychiatric illness with a markedly pronounced genetic and neurobiological basis, marked by manic or hypomanic episodes (elevated or irritable mood, increased drive, reduced need for sleep, grandiosity, risky behavior) alternating with depressive episodes (depressed mood, lack of drive, loss of interest, and in severe cases suicidal thoughts). Between episodes, mood can remain stable for extended periods. The illness arises from a complex interplay of genetic predisposition and neurobiological factors in mood-regulating circuits; stress and sleep deprivation can trigger episodes but are not the cause of the underlying illness. Manic episodes are sometimes initially experienced as pleasant by those affected, but must be taken medically seriously, since they can lead to considerable social, financial, and health consequences; the depressive phases, correspondingly, are by no means 'just' the counterbalance to that, but independently and severely distressing in their own right.
Typische Symptome: Manic/hypomanic episodes: elevated or irritable mood, grandiosity; Reduced need for sleep during manic phases without exhaustion; Increased drive and risky, impulsive behavior during mania; Depressive episodes: depressed mood, lack of drive; Loss of interest and exhaustion during depressive phases; Marked swings between episodes; In severe cases, psychotic symptoms during extreme episodes
Notfall-Hinweis: In the event of acute mania with risk of harm to self or others, acute suicidal thoughts during a depressive phase, or psychotic symptoms, call emergency services immediately or go to the nearest psychiatric emergency room; for acute suicidal thoughts, also contact a crisis line (in the US: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, call or text 988).
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner. Bipolar disorder is a severe neurobiological illness; personality or subtype has no causal influence whatsoever on who develops it.
To state this unmistakably up front: bipolar disorder is not caused by personality, temperament, or any particular subtype – it has a strong genetic and neurobiological basis, and no personality model can predict who will develop it. No subtype carries a special vulnerability here. What this section describes is therefore explicitly not the origin of the illness, but how different people experience and cope with their manic and depressive phases, how they relate to medication, and how they handle stigma – without glamorizing mania or downplaying the depressive phases, since both must be taken seriously in their own right. Each of the 27 subtypes shows its own pattern here in coping with the illness, never in causing it.
--- Typ 1: A way of handling loss of control in both directions ---
SE1: In a manic phase, of all things, the self-preservation One's usually reliable self-control can slip away, which can lead to deep shame once the episode subsides. In the depressive phase, strict self-condemnation often returns.
SO1: Behavior during a manic episode that violates her own moral standards can weigh especially heavily on the social One afterward. Open conversation with the treatment team about this shame matters here.
SX1: The sexual One shows her reactions in both phases directly to the one important person rather than hiding them. This openness can help her carry even difficult episodes together with someone.
--- Typ 2: A way of handling relationship through both phases ---
SE2: In a manic phase, the self-preservation Two can impulsively overextend her caregiving for others; in the depressive phase, by contrast, she often feels unable to be there for anyone at all. Both extremes can trigger considerable guilt.
SO2: During a manic episode, the social Two can impulsively widen her attentiveness toward many people, which often leaves her overwhelmed once the episode passes. In depression, she instead tends to withdraw completely.
SX2: The sexual Two experiences both phases most intensely in the context of the one important relationship. This one solid bond can be stabilizing during mania as well as sustaining during depression.
--- Typ 3: A way of handling achievement through both phases ---
SE3: In a manic phase, the self-preservation Three's heightened energy can at first look like extraordinary productivity, until risky decisions make the consequences visible. The depressive phase afterward hits her self-worth especially hard.
